explain.why: “Look!” and “right now. You can smell it” indicate an ongoing action. Therefore, “is preparing” is appropriate.
explain.rule:
Distinguish ROUTINE vs. CONTINUOUS:
1. Routine / repeated habit: Use Present Simple (Verb 1). Indicated by: every day, always, usually.
2. Happening right now: Use Present Continuous (am/is/are + Verb-ing). Indicated by: right now, at the moment, Look!, Listen!

💡 QUICK FORMULA:
Happening NOW ➡️ Use am/is/are + Verb-ing (example: is eating right now).
Habit / routine schedule ➡️ Use Verb 1 (-s/-es) (example: eats every day).
State verbs (know, like, want, understand) ➡️ Always use Present Simple, never use -ing!
explain.memory: The presence of “Look!” indicates using the -ing form.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

prepares.whyFails: 'Prepares' states a routine or general habit, which clashes with a dish being made at this very moment.

has prepared.whyFails: 'Has prepared' announces a finished dish, but 'right now. You can smell it' shows the cooking is still in progress.

prepare.whyFails: Third-person singular subject requires an -s or auxiliary form, not the bare infinitive.

explain.why: “in 2019” is a closed time frame, so the past simple is used, not the present perfect.
explain.rule: The present perfect cannot be used with a specific past time expression. Examples include “yesterday”, “in 2019”, or “last week”.
explain.memory: A specific date means past simple.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

was traveling.whyFails: Past continuous frames an ongoing background action, not a completed single event.
was traveling.misconception: aspect confusion (progressive for a single completed trip)

travels.whyFails: Present simple cannot refer to a dated past event.

explain.why: “Will” is used for decisions made at the moment of speaking, such as offering help.
explain.rule:
Distinguishing future plans vs. spontaneous decisions / guesses:
• “be going to” is used for plans or intentions decided beforehand, or when there is clear evidence right in front of you.
• “will” is used for spontaneous decisions made at the moment of speaking, promises, or guesses without evidence.

💡 QUICK FORMULA:
Planned / evidence in sight ➡️ Use am/is/are going to.
Sudden decision / offer / personal guess ➡️ Use will + Verb 1.
After both ➡️ The verb always returns to the bare Verb 1.
explain.memory: For an instant decision, use “will” instantly.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

am getting.misconception: treats spontaneous offers as pre-arranged plans

get.whyFails: Present simple is for routines/schedules, not spontaneous offers.
get.misconception: present simple used for a one-off future act

am going to getting.whyFails: 'Going to' takes the base verb, not another -ing form.

explain.why: The sentence states this is a museum rule, not a choice. That is a characteristic of obligation.
explain.rule: “Must” and “have to” express obligation. “Can”, “may”, and “could” express permission or possibility.
explain.memory: If it is a rule, use “must”.
explain.avoid: Pay attention to the level of necessity: use “must” for strong obligations/official rules.

may.whyFails: 'May' grants permission; it does not impose a requirement.

could.whyFails: 'Could' softens a request or suggests possibility, not a firm rule.
could.misconception: obligation read as a polite hypothetical

explain.why: “Can’t” expresses a negative deduction you are very sure of based on available evidence.
explain.rule: To make a negative deduction you are sure of, use “can’t”, not “mustn't” which means prohibition.
explain.memory: Convinced it's impossible: use “can’t”, not “mustn't”.
explain.avoid: For a negative logical deduction (certainly not), use “can't”, not “mustn't”.

mustn't.whyFails: 'Mustn't' expresses prohibition ('not allowed to'), not a deduction that something is impossible.
mustn't.misconception: negative obligation confused with negative deduction

explain.why: Heating ice always causes it to melt, not just once. Facts like this use the present simple in both clauses.
explain.rule:
For certain facts or laws of nature: Both use ordinary verbs without “will”. Example: If you heat ice, it melts.
For future possibilities or plans: The “if” clause uses the ordinary verb, and the consequence uses “will”. Example: If it rains tomorrow, we will stay home.

💡 QUICK FORMULA:
Certain fact / always true ➡️ If + Verb 1, Verb 1 (without will).
Future possibility ➡️ If + Verb 1, will + Verb 1.
explain.memory: Always true? Present meets present.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

will melt.whyFails: This is correct English, but 'will' frames it as a prediction about a particular occasion; the question asks for the always-true general fact.
will melt.misconception: general truth treated as a one-time prediction

would melt.whyFails: 'Would' signals an unreal/hypothetical condition, but heating ice always causes melting: it's real and general.

melted.whyFails: Zero conditional describes a general truth in present tense, not a completed past event.
melted.misconception: past tense used for a timeless fact

explain.why: The sentence states that winning the lottery will not happen. Such unreal situations use the past simple in the if-clause.
explain.rule:
For real future possibilities: Use standard conditional sentences (If + Verb 1, will).
For purely imagined or currently impossible dreams: The “if” clause uses Verb 2, and the result uses “would” + base verb. Example: If I won the lottery, I would travel the world (Reality is I haven't won and don't have the money).

💡 QUICK FORMULA:
Currently unreal imagination ➡️ If + Verb 2, would + Verb 1.
Subject meets the verb “be” ➡️ Universally use were (example: If I were you).
explain.memory: Unreal now: past form, non-past meaning.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

win.whyFails: First-conditional 'if + present' should not pair with 'would' in the result clause.
win.misconception: if-clause verb form mismatched with 'would' in the main clause

would win.whyFails: Standard conditionals put 'would' only in the result clause, not the if-clause.

will win.whyFails: The speaker explicitly signals this is not going to happen, which calls for the unreal second conditional, not 'will'.
will win.misconception: real/likely framing applied to an admittedly unlikely event

explain.why: The passive without the “by” phrase is more appropriate when the doer is unknown or unimportant.
explain.rule:
For active sentences (doer performs the action): The subject at the front does something. Example: Budi repaired the bike.
For passive sentences (subject receives the action): Must include the verb “be” (is/am/are or was/were) + past participle (Verb 3). Example: The bike was repaired by Budi.

💡 QUICK FORMULA:
Active sentence ➡️ Subject performs the action (example: They built the house).
Passive sentence ➡️ Must use am/is/are/was/were + Verb 3 (example: The house was built).
Present time uses is/am/are + Verb 3, past time uses was/were + Verb 3.
explain.memory: If you don't know who the doer is, drop the “by”.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

constructed.whyFails: Using active voice would require naming a subject/agent, but the context states the builder is unknown.
constructed.misconception: active voice used despite an unknown/irrelevant agent

has construct.whyFails: This is not a valid English verb form.

was constructed by workers.whyFails: 'By workers' names a vague builder that adds nothing: the sentence says nobody knows who built it, so leave the agent out.
was constructed by workers.misconception: adds a vague, uninformative agent instead of omitting it

explain.why: The reporting verb “said” and time expression “Yesterday” place the report in the past, and the situation is already over. Therefore, “am” shifts back to “was”.
explain.rule:
For direct speech: Uses quotation marks exactly as spoken. Example: He said, “I am happy”.
For reported speech with a past reporting verb (said / told): The tense of the utterance must shift one step back into the past (backshift). Verb 1 shifts to Verb 2, “am/is” becomes “was”, “will” becomes “would”, and “can” becomes “could”. Example: He said that he was happy.
Difference between Say and Tell: With “said”, follow directly with the clause (She said that...). With “told”, you MUST mention the listener (She told me that...).

💡 QUICK FORMULA:
Past reporting verb (said/told) ➡️ Tenses inside shift back one step (V1 ➡️ V2, will ➡️ would, can ➡️ could).
With a listener ➡️ Use told + person (example: told me, not said me ❌).
Without mentioning a person ➡️ Use said (that).
explain.memory: Neutral reporting usually shifts one step back.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

is.whyFails: Since the reporting verb 'said' is past, the reported present tense must shift back to past.

has been.whyFails: Present simple in direct speech backshifts to past simple, not present perfect.
has been.misconception: backshift target confused with present perfect

will be.whyFails: This changes present into future rather than shifting it one step back into the past.
will be.misconception: tense category changed instead of shifted one step back

explain.why: “Stop to buy” means he stops briefly in order to buy bread, so the to-infinitive expresses purpose.
explain.rule: “Stop” + -ing form means you stop doing that activity. “Stop” + to + verb means stopping briefly to do something else.
explain.memory: “Stop to do” means stopping for a specific purpose.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

buying.whyFails: 'Stop buying' would mean she quit the habit of buying bread, which contradicts the context of a single errand.
buying.misconception: gerund used where a purpose-infinitive is needed

buy.whyFails: The purpose sense of 'stop' requires a to-infinitive, not a bare form.
buy.misconception: bare infinitive used instead of the required to-infinitive

having bought.whyFails: This form implies a completed prior action rather than the purpose of stopping.
having bought.misconception: perfect gerund used where a simple purpose clause is needed

explain.why: The structure “more scenic ... than” compares exactly two paths. That is the function of the comparative form.
explain.rule: The comparative form works with “than” to compare two things. The superlative form uses "the" plus -est or most to indicate the number one in a group.
explain.memory: Two things use -er or more. A group uses -est or most.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

the most scenic.whyFails: Superlatives compare three or more items; here only two routes are being compared.
the most scenic.misconception: superlative used for a two-item comparison

scenic.whyFails: 'Scenic' leaves the adjective unmarked, so the 'than' comparison has nothing to hang on.
scenic.misconception: base adjective used without comparative marking

most scenic.whyFails: Besides missing 'the', a superlative is still the wrong category for a two-item comparison.
most scenic.misconception: superlative used without 'the', still wrong scope

explain.why: “haven’t” in the main clause is negative and the auxiliary verb is “have”. Therefore, the tag is positive and retains “have”.
explain.rule: Question tags typically reverse the positive-negative polarity of the main clause and repeat the same auxiliary verb. Tags that match the polarity of the main clause are used to show agreement or surprise, like “So you are coming, are you?”.
explain.memory: Negative sentences usually take a positive tag.
explain.avoid: Check the main clause: if negative (“haven't”), the question tag must be positive (“have you”).

haven't you.whyFails: The main clause is already negative, so the tag must be positive, not also negative.
haven't you.misconception: tag polarity copied instead of reversed

did you.whyFails: The main clause uses present perfect ('haven't'), so the tag must use 'have', not 'did'.
did you.misconception: wrong auxiliary borrowed from a different tense

don't you.whyFails: The auxiliary in the tag must match the auxiliary in the statement, which is 'have', not 'do'.
don't you.misconception: wrong auxiliary substituted (present simple instead of present perfect)

explain.why: Cooking was already underway as the background time when the electricity suddenly went out.
explain.rule: Past continuous uses was or were + -ing verb to build the background. Past simple reports the interrupting event.
explain.memory: Background uses -ing, interrupter uses past simple.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

cooked.whyFails: This would suggest the cooking finished before the power went out, losing the interruption meaning.
cooked.misconception: treats both clauses as sequential completed events

have cooked.whyFails: Present perfect has no fixed past time frame like 'when the power went out' requires.
have cooked.misconception: confuses interrupted past action with present perfect result

cook.whyFails: The sentence is anchored in the past by 'went out', so a present bare form is ungrammatical.
cook.misconception: bare present form used for a past narrative

explain.why: “three novels” counts a completed result, and “already working on a fourth” indicates the fourth novel has just begun. Therefore, the present perfect simple is appropriate.
explain.rule: Use the present perfect simple for completed actions whose results are still relevant now. Use the present perfect continuous when emphasizing the duration or repetition of an activity.
explain.memory: Completed results use simple; ongoing processes use continuous.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

has been writing.whyFails: The sentence counts a completed result ('three novels'), which needs the simple form, not the continuous.
has been writing.misconception: over-applies continuous aspect whenever a time span like 'this year' appears

was writing.whyFails: 'Was writing' frames the writing inside a closed past moment, but 'this year' is still open and no finished reference point appears in the sentence.
was writing.misconception: shifts to a fixed past narrative tense

writes.whyFails: The sentence reports a specific cumulative achievement so far, not a general habit.
writes.misconception: treats the sentence as a habitual routine

explain.why: “By the time” plus a past simple clause creates a reference point. Actions completed before that point use the past perfect.
explain.rule: Past perfect uses had + past participle (Verb 3). This form indicates the earlier action between two past events.
explain.memory: With “by the time X happened”, the other clause requires “had” at the front.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

already gave.whyFails: Without past perfect, 'by the time' loses its meaning of 'before this later point'.
already gave.misconception: uses past simple for the earlier event, flattening the sequence

are already giving.whyFails: The past reference point set by 'the ambulance arrived' rules out a present form; the first aid had to be finished before that moment.
are already giving.misconception: keeps the action in progress at 'now' instead of marking it completed before the past reference point

already give.whyFails: The whole sentence is anchored in the past by 'arrived', making the bare present ungrammatical.
already give.misconception: bare present form in a past narrative

explain.why: Dinner was still ongoing at exactly eight o'clock, which is expressed by the future continuous.
explain.rule: Future continuous “will be” + -ing verb describes an action still in progress at a specific time in the future. Future perfect “will have” + past participle (Verb 3) describes an action completed before that time.
explain.memory: Still in progress later uses “will be” + -ing; already completed uses “will have” + Verb 3.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

will have.whyFails: This is correct English ('have dinner' = eat), but it only announces the plan; it does not present the meal as already under way at 8pm.
will have.misconception: uses a bare future form without marking the ongoing nature of the action

will have had.whyFails: The context says dinner is happening AT 8pm, so it isn't finished yet at that point.
will have had.misconception: wrongly applies future perfect, implying the dinner is finished by 8pm

have.whyFails: The sentence explicitly refers to a specific future time ('at 8pm'), which requires a future form.
have.misconception: drops the future marker entirely, defaulting to present simple

explain.why: This is a specific achievement in a difficult situation, so “was/were able to” is appropriate.
explain.rule: Use “could” for general past ability. Use “was/were able to” or “managed to” for a specific single achievement.
explain.memory: Succeeded once in an urgent situation: “was able to”, not “could”.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

could get.whyFails: 'Could' normally reports general past ability, not one specific successful event under pressure.
could get.misconception: extends general-ability 'could' to a single specific achievement

can get.whyFails: The context ('was spreading') anchors the sentence firmly in the past.
can get.misconception: uses present-tense modal for a clearly past narrative

get.whyFails: The sentence needs a modal or auxiliary to express ability, not a bare verb.

explain.why: The lights being out and the car being gone is strong evidence, so it matches “must have” + past participle.
explain.rule:
If 100% certain something DEFINITELY happened in the past: Use “must have + Verb 3”. Example: He must have left already (His car is gone).
If 100% certain something was IMPOSSIBLE to have happened in the past: Use “can't have + Verb 3”. Example: She can't have taken that train (I waited on the platform and didn't see her).

💡 QUICK FORMULA:
Certain it happened ➡️ must have + Verb 3.
Certain it was impossible ➡️ can't have + Verb 3.
explain.memory: Strong supporting evidence: “must have”. Strong contradicting evidence: “can’t have”.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

can't have.whyFails: The evidence (dark house, missing car) supports the conclusion that he DID leave, not that he couldn't have.
can't have.misconception: confuses the polarity of the deduction

should have.whyFails: 'Should have' criticizes a missed obligation; it doesn't express a logical deduction from evidence.
should have.misconception: confuses deduction with obligation/expectation not met

might have.whyFails: The stem gives strong supporting evidence, which calls for the confident 'must have', not a tentative 'might have'.
might have.misconception: weakens certainty when the evidence actually supports a confident conclusion

explain.why: “Needn’t” states something is unnecessary, which matches having a membership card that already suffices.
explain.rule:
If it is OPTIONAL (free to do or not, still permitted): Use “needn't” or “don't have to”. Example: You needn't bring food (It's already provided there).
If STRICTLY PROHIBITED (must not be done due to rules/danger): Use “mustn't”. Example: You mustn't tell anyone.

💡 QUICK FORMULA:
Unnecessary / optional ➡️ needn't (or don't have to).
Strictly prohibited / forbidden ➡️ mustn't (meaning “don't / forbidden”).
explain.memory: “Mustn’t” means you are prohibited from doing something. “Needn’t” means it is optional or unnecessary.
explain.avoid: For things that are not necessary to do, use “needn't” (not the prohibition “mustn't”).

mustn't.whyFails: 'Mustn't' means it is forbidden to bring a passport, which contradicts the neutral context of simply not being required.
mustn't.misconception: treats 'mustn't' as the negation of obligation rather than prohibition

shouldn't.whyFails: The sentence isn't warning against bringing a passport, only saying it isn't required.
shouldn't.misconception: confuses absence of necessity with negative advice

can't.whyFails: Nothing in the context suggests bringing a passport is not allowed, only that it's unnecessary.
can't.misconception: confuses lack of requirement with lack of permission/ability

explain.why: The main clause “wouldn’t have missed” indicates a third conditional about an unreal past. Therefore, the “if” clause requires the past perfect.
explain.rule:
For imaginary conditions in the present: Use If + Verb 2, would + Verb 1.
For regrets about past events: Use “had + Verb 3” in the “if” clause and “would have + Verb 3” in the result clause. Example: If she had woken up earlier, she wouldn't have missed the flight (Fact: she woke up late yesterday and the flight had already departed).

💡 QUICK RULE:
Regretting a past event ➡️ If + had + Verb 3.
The result of the regret ➡️ would have + Verb 3 (or wouldn't have).
explain.memory: Both look back to the past: had ... would have ...
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

left.whyFails: The main clause 'wouldn't have missed' signals a third conditional, which requires 'had left' in the if-clause, not simple past.
left.misconception: uses second-conditional past simple in an if-clause that needs third-conditional past perfect

would leave.whyFails: The if-clause of a conditional never takes 'would'; that belongs only in the main clause.

leaves.whyFails: The sentence discusses a hypothetical about the past, not a general truth or future possibility.
leaves.misconception: uses a zero/first-conditional present form for a past unreal situation

explain.why: The work decision is unreal and in the past, but the word “now” points to the current state. Therefore, “wouldn't be” is the correct choice.
explain.rule: Mixed conditional for a past cause and a present result: if + past perfect, followed by would + base verb.
explain.memory: Past cause, present result: had done → would be.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

wouldn't have been.whyFails: 'Would not have been' is a past hypothetical result, but 'now' requires a present hypothetical state.
wouldn't have been.misconception: places the result in the unreal past instead of the present

weren't.whyFails: 'Weren't' is a bare past simple: it drops the modal 'would' that the result clause of this mixed conditional needs to mark the imagined present outcome.
weren't.misconception: uses a past form without the modal required in the result clause

hadn't been.whyFails: Past perfect belongs in the unreal past condition; it cannot express the present result in the main clause.
hadn't been.misconception: repeats past perfect in the main clause

explain.why: “Unless” already means “if ... not”, so the condition of studying harder connects without an additional negative word.
explain.rule:
If using “if”: You need the negative word “not” for negative conditions. Example: If you don't study, you won't pass.
If using “unless”: It already means “except if” (if ... not), so the verb following it MUST be in the positive form without “not”. Example: Unless you study, you won't pass.

💡 QUICK RULE:
Contains “don't / not” ➡️ Pair with If.
The sentence is positive but has an exclusionary meaning ➡️ Pair with Unless (do not use not again!).
explain.memory: “Unless” already means “if not”; never write “unless not”.
explain.avoid: The clause after “unless” already implies a negative condition; do not add a double negative.

unless not.whyFails: 'Unless' already means 'if not', so adding another 'not' creates a double negative that reverses the intended meaning.
unless not.misconception: stacks a redundant negative onto 'unless', which is already negative in meaning

if not.whyFails: 'If not' typically needs a different clause structure here ('if you don't study harder'); as written, 'unless' fits the sentence pattern, not the bare phrase 'if not' before a full clause.
if not.misconception: confuses 'if not' with 'unless' as directly interchangeable in this exact slot

if.whyFails: Using 'if' alone would mean passing depends on studying, but without the negative link the condition for failing is lost.
if.misconception: drops the negative condition entirely, reversing the sentence's logic

explain.why: The form is the one receiving the signing action, and the modal “must” requires “be” + past participle to make the passive voice correct.
explain.rule:
For modals in active sentences: After a modal (can, must, should, will), use the base verb (Verb 1). Example: You must sign this form.
For modals in passive sentences (meaning 'to be' or 'to get'): After a modal, you MUST insert “be” followed by Verb 3. Example: This form must be signed or Tickets can be bought online.

💡 QUICK RULE:
Active after modal ➡️ modal + Verb 1 (e.g., must sign, can do).
Passive after modal ➡️ modal + be + Verb 3 (e.g., must be signed, can be found).
The word “be” must be in its base form ➡️ Do not change it to is/am/are or been after a modal!
explain.memory: Passive voice with a modal always requires “be” before the past participle.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

must sign.whyFails: This would mean the form itself is doing the signing, not receiving the action.
must sign.misconception: leaves the verb in active form after the modal

must signed.whyFails: Modal passive structure requires 'be' before the past participle; a bare past participle after a modal is ungrammatical.
must signed.misconception: omits the auxiliary 'be' required to form the passive after a modal

must be signing.whyFails: Passive voice requires the past participle ('signed'), not the present participle ('signing').
must be signing.misconception: uses the -ing form instead of the past participle

explain.why: The passive “get” is typical of casual speech. It is usually used for unpleasant events that happen suddenly. This fits the tone of this exclamation.
explain.rule:
Formal/standard passive: Use “be” (is/am/are or was/were) + Verb 3. Example: The bridge was built in 1990 or The document was signed.
Informal/conversational passive: Use “get” + Verb 3, specifically for sudden, unintentional, unfortunate, or physical events. Example: He got hurt, The thief got caught, or get paid.

💡 QUICK RULE:
Formal situations, inanimate objects, or general facts ➡️ Use be + Verb 3.
Casual conversation, sudden/unfortunate/physical events ➡️ Use get / got + Verb 3.
Check the tense ➡️ Past tense uses got + Verb 3, present tense uses get/gets + Verb 3.
explain.memory: Casual, sudden, and unpleasant: use the “get” passive.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

was.whyFails: While 'was stolen' is grammatical, the casual tone ('Ugh') and sudden, unwelcome event pattern strongly cue the 'get' passive as the natural informal choice being tested.
was.misconception: not wrong grammatically, but ignores that the informal, exclamatory register strongly favors the 'get' passive here

has.whyFails: 'Has stolen' does not form a valid passive here; the sentence needs a simple past passive auxiliary.
has.misconception: misapplies present perfect auxiliary to a simple past passive event

did.whyFails: 'Did stolen' is ungrammatical; 'did' cannot combine directly with a past participle to form the passive.
did.misconception: uses an active-voice auxiliary in a passive construction

explain.why: Reported questions drop the inverted word order and the question mark. The order becomes like a statement, and the verb shifts back in tense.
explain.rule:
For WH- Questions (Where, What, Why, How):
In direct speech: The question word is followed by an auxiliary verb. Example: “Where is the station?”.
In reported speech: The question word is kept, but the word order changes to a standard positive sentence: Question Word + Subject + Verb (no question mark and no auxiliary do/does/did). Example: She asked where the station was.

💡 QUICK RULE:
Order after WH- word ➡️ Question Word + Subject + Verb (not question order!).
Do not use auxiliary verbs ➡️ Do not use do/does/did after the question word in reported questions.
Tense shift ➡️ The verb must shift back to the past.
explain.memory: Reported questions sound like statements.
explain.avoid: After the reporting verb, rearrange the subordinate clause like a statement.

did live.whyFails: “did” is unnecessary here; the main verb should simply shift to the past tense.
did live.misconception: keeps 'did' as an unnecessary emphatic auxiliary instead of a simple backshifted past verb

explain.why: Reported commands use the pattern “tell”, “order”, or “ask”, followed by the object, then the “to” infinitive.
explain.rule:
For direct commands: Use a command or prohibition verb. Example: “Open the door!” or “Don't touch that!”.
For reported commands: Use “told” or “asked” + the person + “to” (or “not to”).
Positive command: Use “to + base verb”. Example: The teacher told us to open the book.
Negative prohibition: Use “not to + base verb” (the word “not” must come before “to”). Example: Mum told me not to touch the wet paint.

💡 QUICK RULE:
Telling someone to do something ➡️ told / asked + person + to + Verb 1.
Prohibiting / “Don't” ➡️ told / asked + person + not to + Verb 1.
Strictly forbidden ➡️ Do not use don't to or to don't ❌!
explain.memory: Commands become “told someone TO do it”, not “told that they did it”.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

that they stop talking and listen.whyFails: Commands are reported with the infinitive pattern, not a 'that' clause with a backshifted verb.
that they stop talking and listen.misconception: applies the statement-reporting pattern ('that' clause) to an imperative

they stopped talking and listened.whyFails: This drops the reporting structure entirely and reads as an independent past statement, not a reported command.
they stopped talking and listened.misconception: backshifts as if reporting a past statement rather than a command

stop talking and listen.whyFails: Without 'to' and an object, this is just the original command repeated, not properly reported speech.
stop talking and listen.misconception: leaves the original imperative form unchanged, without integrating it into reported speech

explain.why: “Suggested” fits the meaning of “Why don’t we ...?” and accepts the gerund (-ing form) as its object. There is no person pronoun in between.
explain.rule: “Suggest” is followed by the -ing form or a “that” clause, and does not accept a person as a direct object. Tell, ask, and order are followed by an object then the “to” form.
explain.memory: “Suggest” is followed by the -ing form; never use “suggested me/us to ...”.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

told us.whyFails: 'Why don't we...?' is a suggestion, not a command, so 'told' misrepresents the speech act and also needs a to-infinitive, not '-ing'.
told us.misconception: uses a direct-instruction verb for what was actually a suggestion

ordered us.whyFails: The original utterance is a soft suggestion, and 'ordered' both misstates the tone and needs a to-infinitive, not '-ing'.
ordered us.misconception: escalates a mild suggestion into a forceful command

suggested us.whyFails: 'Suggest' does not take a personal object directly like 'suggested us'; it takes '-ing', a 'that' clause, or 'to someone that...'.
suggested us.misconception: copies the object pattern of 'tell/ask' (verb + object) onto 'suggest', which doesn't take a direct personal object this way

explain.why: “Chairs” can be counted individually and are plural. Therefore, “many” is appropriate for this negative sentence.
explain.rule:
For countable nouns (plural with -s): Pair with “many” or “few”. Example: many chairs, few friends.
For uncountable nouns (water, time, sugar, money): Pair with “much” or “little”. Example: much water, little time.

💡 QUICK RULE:
Countable (has plural -s) ➡️ Use many or few.
Uncountable (liquids, powders, time) ➡️ Use much or little.
explain.memory: Countable: many or few. Uncountable: much or little.
explain.avoid: For countable nouns in the plural form (chairs), use “many”, not “much”.

much.whyFails: 'Much' presupposes an uncountable mass noun, but 'chairs' names things you can count one by one, so the pairing collapses.
much.misconception: applies the uncountable-noun quantifier to a countable plural noun

little.whyFails: 'Little' pairs with uncountable nouns (little water), not countable plural nouns like 'chairs', which need 'few'.
little.misconception: applies the uncountable-noun quantifier ('little') to a countable plural noun, and also confuses scarcity type

much of.whyFails: 'Much of' requires a specific defined noun phrase (much of the furniture) and still wouldn't fix the countable/uncountable mismatch.
much of.misconception: adds an unnecessary partitive 'of' without a following determiner, and still misapplies 'much' to a countable noun

explain.why: The -ing form “locking” expresses the memory of an action that is already finished, which fits with “this morning”.
explain.rule: “Remember” + -ing means remembering something that already happened. “Remember” + to means not forgetting to do something later.
explain.memory: “Remember doing” is a past memory; “remember to do” is a future task.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

to lock.whyFails: 'Remember to lock' would mean not forgetting a future duty, but the sentence clearly recalls something that already happened this morning.
to lock.misconception: applies the 'future duty' pattern ('remember to do') to a sentence that is actually recalling a completed past action

lock.whyFails: 'Remember' takes either a gerund or a to-infinitive, never a bare infinitive.
lock.misconception: uses the bare infinitive, which isn't a valid pattern after 'remember' in either meaning

to have locked.whyFails: 'Remember to have locked' does not exist as an English pattern; recalling the past act of locking needs the gerund 'locking'.
to have locked.misconception: applies a perfect to-infinitive after 'remember', which English does not use for recalling a past action

explain.why: “To have time to prepare” explains the reason he returned early. This is the purpose infinitive.
explain.rule:
Infinitive of Purpose vs. Preposition + Gerund:
1. Expressing purpose (“in order to”): Use to + base verb. Example: I went to the store to buy milk (Not for buy ❌ and not for buying ❌).
2. After prepositions other than 'to' (for, about, without, after): The verb must use the -ing suffix. Example: This tool is used for cutting paper.

💡 QUICK RULE:
Expressing the purpose of an action ➡️ to + Verb 1 (e.g., came to help).
After common prepositions (for, without, about, by) ➡️ preposition + Verb-ing.
Prohibition ➡️ Do not use for + Verb 1 (wrong: came for help you ❌).
explain.memory: Purpose is expressed simply by “to” plus the verb, without a preposition.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

for having.whyFails: The sentence expresses WHY she left early (purpose), which needs a to-infinitive, not a preposition + gerund pattern.
for having.misconception: misreads the sentence as needing a preposition + gerund structure instead of an infinitive of purpose

for to have.whyFails: English does not use 'for to' before a base verb to express purpose; the infinitive of purpose stands alone with 'to'.
for to have.misconception: mixes a preposition with a to-infinitive, a combination that isn't standard in English

having.whyFails: Without 'to', the sentence loses the explicit purpose meaning and becomes grammatically incomplete in this slot.
having.misconception: drops the purpose marker entirely, leaving a bare gerund with no clear grammatical link to the main clause

explain.why: “Whose” emphasizes that the “latest novel” belongs to the author, so the possession is connected.
explain.rule:
To connect a person with THEIR POSSESSION (meaning “whose ...”): You must use “whose” and follow it immediately with the noun without an article (a/the). Example: That's the boy whose phone was lost.
Compare with “who” (the doer: the boy who called me) and “who's” (contraction of who is / who has: the boy who's standing there).

💡 QUICK RULE:
There is a noun after the blank ➡️ Must choose whose (e.g., whose car).
There is an action verb after the blank ➡️ Choose who.
There is an apostrophe (who's) ➡️ That is who is, NOT for possession!
explain.memory: “Whose” means possession; “who’s” means who is or who has.
explain.avoid: To express the possessive relationship of a person to their object, use “whose”, not “who” or “which”.

who's.whyFails: 'Who's' means 'who is' or 'who has', which doesn't fit before a possessed noun like 'latest novel'.
who's.misconception: confuses the contraction 'who's' (who is / who has) with the possessive relative pronoun 'whose'

who.whyFails: 'Who' alone cannot show that the novel belongs to the author; the sentence needs the possessive form.
who.misconception: uses the subject relative pronoun without showing the required possessive relationship

which.whyFails: 'Which' refers to things, not people, so it can't correctly refer back to 'the author'.
which.misconception: uses the non-personal relative pronoun for a person (the author)

explain.why: Two laptops need the exact same amount of time, ten seconds. Therefore, only the equal form “as fast as” is suitable.
explain.rule: The pattern as + adjective + as states two things are equal. The comparative form with “than” indicates a difference.
explain.memory: Exactly the same means there is no difference, so use as ... as.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

faster than.whyFails: The sentence states both laptops take exactly the same time, so a comparative claiming one is faster contradicts the given fact.
faster than.misconception: defaults to the comparative form even though the context implies equality, not difference

the fastest.whyFails: Only two laptops are being compared, and the superlative wrongly implies a comparison among a larger group.
the fastest.misconception: confuses a two-item comparison with a superlative among three or more items

more fast than.whyFails: 'Fast' is a short adjective that forms its comparative with '-er' (faster), not with 'more'.
more fast than.misconception: applies the periphrastic 'more + adjective' pattern to a short one-syllable adjective that takes '-er'

explain.why: “As the deadline approached” indicates a gradual and continuous increase. The double comparative “busier and busier” expresses that meaning.
explain.rule: The pattern comparative + and + comparative expresses a continuous change. Examples: “busier and busier” or “more and more difficult”.
explain.memory: Continuous change doubles the comparative form.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

busier than before.whyFails: This is correct English, but it compares against one earlier point; the question asks for the form that shows the increase continuing step by step.
busier than before.misconception: treats a continuous, ongoing change as a single fixed-point comparison

the busiest.whyFails: The sentence isn't ranking this schedule against other schedules; it's describing continuous change over time.
the busiest.misconception: confuses a progressive change over time with a superlative ranking among multiple items

more busy than usual.whyFails: 'Busy' typically takes '-er' (busier), and the sentence needs the doubled form to show continuous increase, not a comparison to what's usual.
more busy than usual.misconception: uses a single comparative with 'more' for a short adjective, and frames it as a comparison to a norm rather than ongoing change

explain.why: “Didn’t you sleep ...” shows surprise at a face that looks tired. The auxiliary is in the past, so it fits with “last night”.
explain.rule: Negative questions like “Didn’t you ...?” often show surprise or expect agreement. The auxiliary must still match the time reference of the sentence.
explain.memory: A tired face plus “last night” requires the question “didn’t”, not “do”.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

Do.whyFails: A plain 'Do you sleep...' loses the nuance of surprise implied by 'You look exhausted', which fits a negative question better.
Do.misconception: uses a neutral positive question form, missing the speaker's implied surprise/assumption

Don't.whyFails: 'Last night' anchors the question in the past, so the auxiliary must be past tense ('didn't'), not present ('don't').
Don't.misconception: uses present-tense negative auxiliary in a context that requires the past tense to match 'last night'

Aren't.whyFails: 'Sleep' is a regular main verb requiring 'do/did' support in questions, not the 'be' auxiliary.
Aren't.misconception: uses the 'be' auxiliary instead of the 'do' auxiliary needed for the main verb 'sleep'

explain.why: Inside the polite frame “could you tell me ...”, the order reverts to a statement. Subject first, verb follows, and “is” remains in the present.
explain.rule: Polite questions like “Could you tell me ...” insert the question using standard statement word order, without inversion.
explain.memory: Polite questions that are embedded sound like statements: subject first, verb follows.
explain.avoid: After a polite frame, rearrange the subordinate clause into a statement, not a direct question.

pharmacy was.whyFails: there is no past reporting here; the pharmacy's location is a present fact.
pharmacy was.misconception: unnecessarily backshifts to past tense when the pharmacy's existence is a current, general fact

explain.why: “Would” + base verb expresses an event that was still in the future when measured from 2010. It is told from a later perspective.
explain.rule: The future seen from the past uses would or was going to + verb. This describes what followed after a point in the past.
explain.memory: A past point plus “would” means a future that has now already happened.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

was transforming.whyFails: Past continuous describes an action in progress at that past moment, not a later outcome viewed from the past.
was transforming.misconception: confusing future-in-the-past with past continuous background action

will transform.whyFails: The whole sentence is anchored in past time ('In 2010'), so a present-anchored future modal is inconsistent.
will transform.misconception: using present-tense future modal inside a past narrative frame

transformed.whyFails: Simple past would state the transformation as an established past fact, losing the 'seen from an earlier viewpoint' meaning the sentence needs.

explain.why: Past perfect continuous highlights the duration of studying as the direct cause of the red eyes.
explain.rule: Past perfect continuous takes the form had been + verb -ing. It is used for a duration before a point in the past, especially if that duration explains a visible result.
explain.memory: Reddened eyes require a duration-based cause: “had been -ing”.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

had studied.whyFails: This is correct English and does mark the earlier time, but it stresses that the studying was finished rather than how long it accumulated.
had studied.misconception: treating past perfect simple as sufficient for any earlier past event

studied.whyFails: This is correct English ('because' already marks the cause), but it reports the fact plainly instead of foregrounding how long the studying went on.
studied.misconception: using simple past for a state that must be shown as prior to another past moment

was studying.whyFails: Past continuous places the action at the same time as another past event, not clearly before it as the cause of a later result.
was studying.misconception: confusing past continuous with past perfect continuous

explain.why: “Had better” is used for urgent advice where the negative consequences are clearly stated.
explain.rule:
For casual, relaxed advice: Use “should” (followed directly by a verb) or “ought to” (must include “to”). Examples: You should rest or You ought to see a doctor.
For strict/urgent warnings (you will face trouble if ignored): Use “had better” (followed directly by a verb without “to”). Example: You had better leave now (It is better for you to go now, rather than missing the train).

💡 QUICK FORMULA:
There is a “to” after the blanks ➡️ Choose ought (because it pairs with ought to).
Serious/emergency warning ➡️ Use had better + base verb.
Casual advice without “to” ➡️ Use should + base verb.
explain.memory: The last train arrives tomorrow, meaning “had better” applies to today.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

should.whyFails: 'Should' gives general advice but doesn't carry the specific-consequence-if-ignored force the 'if you miss...' clause signals.
should.misconception: treating general advice modal as equally strong as urgent-consequence modal

could.whyFails: 'Could' only suggests an option, not the strong urgency implied by the stated consequence.
could.misconception: using a possibility modal where obligation/urgency is meant

might.whyFails: 'Might' expresses uncertainty about a future event, not advice with an urgent consequence.
might.misconception: using a modal of weak possibility for a directive

explain.why: “Might” expresses a guess with current uncertainty, which matches “I’m not sure”.
explain.rule: “May”, “might”, and “could” plus a base verb express weak possibility regarding the present. “Must” expresses a strong conclusion, while “will” expresses a confident prediction.
explain.memory: “Not sure” pairs with “might”, not “will”.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

will.whyFails: 'Will' asserts confident certainty, which conflicts with the stated 'I'm not sure'.
will.misconception: using the confident future/prediction modal for uncertain present speculation

must.whyFails: 'Must' signals a confident logical conclusion from evidence, stronger than the tentative guess the sentence expresses.
must.misconception: using the strong-deduction modal where only weak possibility is intended

can.whyFails: 'Can' expresses general possibility/ability, not a specific tentative guess about what's happening right now.
can.misconception: using 'can' for a specific present possibility about one situation

explain.why: “Shouldn’t have stayed” criticizes an action that actually happened, namely staying up late, which is the cause of today's fatigue.
explain.rule:
If you regret something that was NOT done (but should have been): Use “should have + Verb 3”. Example: We should have told them (We should have told them yesterday, but we stayed silent).
If you regret something that WAS done (but should not have been): Use “shouldn't have + Verb 3”. Example: He shouldn't have stayed up so late (He shouldn't have stayed up late last night; now he is exhausted).

💡 QUICK FORMULA:
Should have done it but missed it ➡️ should have + Verb 3.
Should not have done it but did it anyway ➡️ shouldn't have + Verb 3.
explain.memory: Fatigue today implies staying up late last night, so use “shouldn’t have”.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

should have stayed.whyFails: This wrongly implies he DIDN'T stay up late, when the context shows he did and that was the mistake.
should have stayed.misconception: missing the negation needed for criticizing a completed unwise action

should stay.whyFails: The event (staying up) is already finished and being judged in hindsight, which requires 'should have + past participle', not present 'should'.
should stay.misconception: using present-form advice modal instead of past-regret structure

wouldn't have stayed.whyFails: 'Wouldn't have' belongs to hypothetical conditional results, not a direct criticism of a real past action.
wouldn't have stayed.misconception: confusing third conditional result clause with a past-regret judgement

explain.why: “Had I known” is the formal inverted form of “If I had known”, commonly used in formal third conditional structures.
explain.rule:
For standard past hypothetical situations (Third Conditional): Use “If” + had + Verb 3. Example: If I had known about the test, I would have studied.
For formal/literary versions (Inversion without “if”): The word “if” is REMOVED, and the auxiliary “Had” is moved to the very front before the subject! Pattern: “Had” + Subject + Verb 3. Example: Had I known about the test, I would have studied (the meaning is identical, but the style is more elegant and formal).

💡 QUICK FORMULA:
Using “if” ➡️ If + Subject + had + Verb 3.
Without “if” (past hypothetical inversion) ➡️ Had + Subject + Verb 3 (the word 'if' is forbidden!).
The result clause remains the same ➡️ Continue using would have + Verb 3.
explain.memory: Remove “if” and invert the order: “Had I known” is equivalent to “If I had known”.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

If had I.whyFails: Formal inversion replaces 'if' entirely: combining both 'if' and inverted word order is redundant and ungrammatical.
If had I.misconception: mixing formal inversion with the conjunction 'if' at the same time

I had.whyFails: Without 'if', normal word order 'I had known' cannot function as a conditional clause on its own.
I had.misconception: using normal subject-verb order, missing the inversion signal

Would I have.whyFails: 'Would' belongs in the result clause ('I would have booked'), not the condition clause, which needs 'had'.
Would I have.misconception: using the result-clause auxiliary structure at the start of the if-clause

explain.why: “Otherwise” here carries the meaning “if the bridge were not closed”. Therefore, it requires a third conditional form.
explain.rule: “Otherwise” can imply an unreal condition. The following clause uses the result form corresponding to the time of that hidden condition.
explain.memory: “Otherwise” is a hidden “if not”, so it often requires “would have + past participle”.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

will be.whyFails: The sentence describes a hypothetical past outcome (a trip that didn't happen shorter), not a real future event.
will be.misconception: reading 'otherwise' as a simple future contrast marker

was.whyFails: Simple past would claim the trip actually was shorter, contradicting the fact that the bridge was closed.
was.misconception: treating the implied condition as a real past fact rather than a hypothetical one

is.whyFails: Present tense doesn't match the past hypothetical scenario the sentence is describing.
is.misconception: ignoring the past time frame set by 'was closed'

explain.why: “It is believed that ...” is a standard passive reporting structure without a specific agent. It is used for widely held beliefs where the source is unclear.
explain.rule: Passive reporting without an agent: It + is or was + past participle + that clause. The dummy subject “it” is always singular.
explain.memory: Without a cited source and with a formal tone: “It is believed that ...”.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

They are believing.whyFails: 'Believe' isn't normally used in continuous form for a general, ongoing belief, and 'they' isn't specified anywhere in context.
They are believing.misconception: using active voice with a vague 'they' plus an incorrect continuous form for a general belief

It believes.whyFails: 'It' is a dummy subject here; it cannot actively 'believe' something, only serve as the subject of the passive construction.
It believes.misconception: treating 'it' as an active subject capable of believing

Is believed.whyFails: The impersonal passive pattern requires 'It is believed that...'; without 'it', the sentence has no grammatical subject.
Is believed.misconception: dropping the required dummy subject 'it' from the impersonal passive pattern

explain.why: The policy is the object of the announcement, so the passive infinitive “to be announced” is required after “is expected”.
explain.rule:
When following verbs that require an infinitive (such as expect to, hope to, need to, deserve to) in the passive voice:
After the word “to”, you MUST pair it with a plain “be” + past participle (Verb 3).
Compare:
- Active: I expect to meet them.
- Passive: Everyone expects to be treated fairly (not to treat and not to being treated).

💡 QUICK FORMULA:
Passive meaning (being acted upon) after “to” ➡️ Must use to be + Verb 3.
Active form (performing the action) ➡️ Use to + Verb 1.
The form of 'be' ➡️ Must be a plain be (forbidden to use to been or to being!).
explain.memory: The policy is being announced, not announcing: “to be announced”.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

to announce.whyFails: 'To announce' makes the policy the announcer, even though the policy is the thing receiving the announcement.
to announce.misconception: using active infinitive when the subject (the policy) cannot perform the announcing itself

announcing.whyFails: 'Expected' takes a to-infinitive complement, not a gerund, regardless of voice.
announcing.misconception: using a gerund where an infinitive pattern after 'expected' is required

to be announcing.whyFails: 'To be announcing' stretches a one-off announcement into an ongoing process that the sentence never describes.
to be announcing.misconception: adding continuous aspect to the passive infinitive unnecessarily

explain.why: “That day” refers back to the day Maria mentioned, which was Monday, from the current perspective.
explain.rule: In reported speech, time and place markers shift: “today” becomes “that day”, “here” becomes “there”, “tomorrow” becomes “the next day”.
explain.memory: The verb shifts back, and “today” also shifts to “that day”.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

today.whyFails: 'Today' only made sense on the actual Monday she spoke; a week later, 'today' would wrongly refer to the current day of reporting.
today.misconception: leaving the original deictic time word unchanged despite the shift in reporting time

tomorrow.whyFails: Maria said 'today', meaning the same day she was speaking (Monday), not the following day.
tomorrow.misconception: misreading the original 'today' as if it referred to the day after speaking

the day.whyFails: 'The day' alone isn't a grammatical time reference here; the correct shifted form needs 'that day' to point back to the specific Monday.
the day.misconception: producing an incomplete deictic shift missing the demonstrative

explain.why: “Books” are plural. “Over there” indicates the objects are far away. “Those” is appropriate for both.
explain.rule: this is for one object nearby. that is for one object far away. these is for many objects nearby. those is for many objects far away.
explain.memory: Plural and far: “those books over there”.
explain.avoid: For plural objects in a distant position (“over there”), use “those”, not “these”.

this.whyFails: 'Books' is plural and 'over there' signals distance, but 'this' is singular and near.
this.misconception: using a singular near demonstrative with a plural, distant noun

that.whyFails: 'That' correctly signals distance but is singular, while 'books' requires a plural determiner.
that.misconception: correctly matching distance but ignoring plural agreement

these.whyFails: 'These' correctly matches the plural noun but wrongly signals nearness, contradicting 'over there'.
these.misconception: correctly matching plural but ignoring the distance cue

explain.why: “Put off” specifically means to delay something to a later time, which fits “until next Thursday”.
explain.rule: Particles in phrasal verbs are not interchangeable. The same verb plus a different particle can create a vastly different meaning.
explain.memory: “Put off” a meeting means to push the schedule further into the future.
explain.avoid: The phrasal verb pair for delaying a meeting is “put off”, not “put out” or “put on”.

down.whyFails: 'Put down' means to physically set something down, write it, or criticize someone, none of which fits 'until next Thursday'.
down.misconception: confusing 'put down' (to set something down / write something / criticize) with 'put off' (postpone)

up.whyFails: 'Put up' means to build/display something or tolerate a situation, not to delay a meeting to a later date.
up.misconception: confusing 'put up' (to erect / accommodate / tolerate) with 'put off' (postpone)

away.whyFails: 'Put away' means to store or tidy something, which doesn't match rescheduling a meeting to a future date.
away.misconception: confusing 'put away' (to store something) with 'put off' (postpone)

explain.why: The fence gap is narrow and enclosed, entered from one side. “Through” indicates movement entering and exiting on the other side.
explain.rule: “Through” is for penetrating an enclosed space. “Across” is for crossing a flat, open surface. “Along” is for following the length of something. “Over” is for passing above something.
explain.memory: A gap has an interior, so it is penetrated using “through”.
explain.avoid: To pass through a gap or narrow space from one side to the other, use the preposition “through”.

across.whyFails: 'Across' moves over an open flat expanse such as a road or a field; a narrow gap has no surface to cross.
across.misconception: using the flat-open-surface preposition for an enclosed three-dimensional space

along.whyFails: 'Along' follows the length of something like a path or a river; squeezing 'along a gap' would mean travelling lengthwise inside it, not passing to the other side.
along.misconception: using the linear-edge preposition (following a line such as a river or street) for movement inside an enclosed space

over.whyFails: 'Over' would mean climbing above the fence, but the sentence describes using the gap in it.
over.misconception: using the above-and-across preposition for movement inside a space, not above it

explain.why: “Try restarting” means attempting a restart as a possible solution. This fits the advice for a file that will not open.
explain.rule: “Try” + -ing form means attempting an action as a possible solution. “Try” + to means making an effort to do something difficult.
explain.memory: Observe the effort: distinguish between trying hard to overcome a difficulty and simply testing a new method.
explain.avoid: Question: is this offered as a solution to be tested, or a difficult task that must be struggled through?

to restart.whyFails: 'Try to restart' would suggest restarting itself is a difficult challenge, but the sentence is suggesting an easy solution to experiment with.
to restart.misconception: using 'try to' (make a difficult effort) where 'try -ing' (experiment with a solution) is meant

restart.whyFails: 'Try' requires either a gerund or a to-infinitive complement, never a bare base form.
restart.misconception: using the bare infinitive after 'try', which isn't a valid pattern

having restarted.whyFails: The sentence is suggesting an action to try now, not referring back to something already done.
having restarted.misconception: using a perfect gerund, implying the action is already completed

explain.why: “Too hot to drink” uses the standard pattern “too” + adjective + “to” form. The level of heat makes drinking it immediately impossible.
explain.rule: The pattern “too” + adjective + “to” form indicates an excessive level. The result is that an action cannot be performed. If the actor needs to be mentioned, insert “for” + the person before the “to” form.
explain.memory: After “too” + adjective, it is always followed by “to”.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

drinking.whyFails: 'Too + adjective' is completed by a to-infinitive, not a gerund, to express the result of the excessive degree.
drinking.misconception: using a gerund where the too/enough + adjective structure requires a to-infinitive

for drinking.whyFails: The too + adjective + to-infinitive pattern doesn't take 'for' before the verb; 'for' is only used before a noun/pronoun subject of the infinitive, not before the verb itself.
for drinking.misconception: inserting an unnecessary preposition before the verb form

drink.whyFails: The too/enough structure specifically requires 'to' before the base verb, not a bare infinitive.
drink.misconception: using the bare infinitive instead of the required to-infinitive

explain.why: “With whom” is the correct formal structure: a preposition followed by the object form “whom” for people.
explain.rule:
When a relative clause requires a preposition (such as to, with, for, about):
1. Conversational / Casual Style: The preposition is placed at the VERY END of the clause. The connector can be “who”, “that”, or omitted. Examples: The girl (who) I talked with or The chair you sat on.
2. Formal Style: The preposition is moved to the FRONT of the connector. If referring to a person, you must use “whom” (not who); if referring to an object, you must use “which” (cannot use that). Examples: The girl with whom I talked or The chair on which you sat.

💡 QUICK FORMULA:
Preposition at the front for PEOPLE ➡️ Must use preposition + whom (e.g., to whom, with whom).
Preposition at the front for OBJECTS ➡️ Must use preposition + which (e.g., in which, on which).
Preposition at the back (casual) ➡️ Connector can be who / that / omitted (e.g., the person I talked to).
explain.memory: A preposition at the front requires “whom”, not “who”.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

with who.whyFails: A preposition placed immediately before the relative pronoun must be followed by the object form 'whom', not the subject form 'who'.
with who.misconception: using subject-form 'who' after a fronted preposition, which requires the object form

who with.whyFails: 'Who with' flips the order, dropping the preposition directly after 'who' in mid-clause ('the colleague who with I was speaking'), an order that is ungrammatical in any register, formal or informal.
who with.misconception: reverses the preposition-pronoun order, putting 'with' directly after 'who' mid-clause

which.whyFails: 'Which' refers to things, not people; 'colleague' is a person and needs a personal relative pronoun.
which.misconception: using the non-personal relative pronoun for a person

explain.why: “Eggs” are plural countable objects. The comparative form for their quantity is “fewer”.
explain.rule: “Fewer” is for plural countable objects. “Less” is for uncountable objects. In casual conversation, “less” is heard more often, but standard usage distinguishes between the two.
explain.memory: Eggs can be counted individually, so use “fewer”.
explain.avoid: For comparing the quantity of countable objects (eggs), use “fewer”, not “less”.

less.whyFails: 'Eggs' is a countable plural noun, and standard usage reserves 'less' for uncountable nouns like 'less sugar' or 'less time'.
less.misconception: applying the uncountable-noun comparative to a countable plural noun

little.whyFails: 'Little' isn't a comparative form at all here; it would need to be 'less' (still wrong for countables) or 'fewer' for a comparison with countables.
little.misconception: using the base uncountable quantifier instead of its comparative form

much less.whyFails: Adding 'much' doesn't fix the underlying countability mismatch: 'eggs' still needs 'fewer', not any form of 'less'.
much less.misconception: intensifying the wrong (uncountable) comparative rather than switching to the countable form

explain.why: “Anything” does not carry a negative meaning itself. Therefore, it is suitable to pair with “didn’t”, which is already negative.
explain.rule: Standard English uses only one negative word per sentence. A negative verb is paired with words starting with “any”, not “no”.
explain.memory: One negative word per sentence: “didn’t ... anything”, not “didn’t ... nothing”.
explain.avoid: In a negative sentence (“didn't find”), use the indefinite pronoun “anything”, not “nothing”.

nothing.whyFails: Standard English negates a clause only once; 'didn't find nothing' doubles the negation, which is non-standard.
nothing.misconception: combining a negated verb ('didn't') with a negative pronoun, creating a non-standard double negative

something.whyFails: 'Something' implies a specific unnamed item exists and was found, which contradicts 'didn't find'.
something.misconception: using a positive indefinite pronoun that contradicts the negative context

no thing.whyFails: 'Nothing' is one word functioning as a negative pronoun; splitting it into 'no thing' isn't standard and still creates double negation with 'didn't'.
no thing.misconception: incorrectly splitting the compound negative pronoun into two words

explain.why: The statement “A” is negative via “don’t enjoy”. Therefore, the agreement must also be in the negative form, which is “Neither do I”.
explain.rule: “So” + auxiliary + subject agrees with a positive statement. “Neither” or “Nor” + auxiliary + subject agrees with a negative statement.
explain.memory: There is a “don’t”, meaning the agreement must also be negative.
explain.avoid: To agree with a negative statement (“don't enjoy”), use “Neither do I”, not “So do I”.

So do.whyFails: 'So do I' is used to agree with a positive statement; A's statement is negative ('don't enjoy'), so it needs the negative agreement form.
So do.misconception: using the positive agreement structure to agree with a negative statement

So does.whyFails: Besides being the wrong polarity for a negative statement, 'does' doesn't agree with the subject 'I'.
So does.misconception: combining the wrong polarity structure with the wrong subject-verb agreement form

Either do.whyFails: 'Either' is used in patterns like 'I don't either', not in the fronted inverted structure that requires 'neither' at the start.
Either do.misconception: confusing 'either' (used with 'not...either' at the end of a clause) with the fronted 'neither' agreement structure

explain.why: The sentence mentions “according to the timetable”, so the schedule is official. Official schedules are expressed using the present simple.
explain.rule: The present simple is used for future events that are fixed by a schedule, program, or calendar. This form does not depend on anyone's personal intention.
explain.memory: Use the present simple for scheduled events.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

is leaving.whyFails: Present continuous typically expresses a personal arrangement someone made, not a fixed timetable set by an external schedule.
is leaving.misconception: using present continuous, associated with personal arrangements, for a fixed external timetable

is going to leave.whyFails: 'Going to' expresses a plan or prediction based on current evidence, not a timetabled fact independent of anyone's intention.
is going to leave.misconception: using 'going to' for intention/prediction rather than an externally fixed schedule

will have left.whyFails: Future perfect would describe the train already having left by some later time, not the scheduled departure time itself.
will have left.misconception: using future perfect, which describes completion before a reference point, not the scheduled departure itself

explain.why: The future perfect continuous form is 'will have been' + verb-ing. This form emphasizes the duration of an activity that continues up to a point in the future.
explain.rule: Use 'will have been' + verb-ing when the duration of time is calculated up to a specific point in the future.
explain.memory: For duration plus a future deadline: use 'will have been' + verb-ing.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

will be working.whyFails: It describes an action in progress at a moment, not accumulated duration leading up to retirement.
will be working.misconception: Confuses future continuous (in-progress at a moment) with future perfect continuous (duration up to a point).

will have worked.whyFails: This is correct English, but it reports the completed fact; the question asks for the form that foregrounds the accumulating duration.
will have worked.misconception: Confuses future perfect simple (completion/result) with future perfect continuous (ongoing duration emphasis).

will work.whyFails: Simple future does not connect the action's duration to the future reference point at all.
will work.misconception: Treats the sentence as a plain future prediction, ignoring the 'by the time' anchor.

explain.why: The past perfect indicates that the train's departure was completed before the speaker arrived, so it is the event that happened first.
explain.rule: Use the past perfect for the earlier of two past events when the sequence needs to be emphasized.
explain.memory: For a past event that happened first, use 'had' + past participle (the 3rd form of the verb).
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

left.whyFails: It fails to mark the train's departure as happening before the arrival, collapsing the flashback into the main timeline.
left.misconception: Treats both events as equally sequential in past simple.

was leaving.whyFails: It would mean the train was in the process of leaving at that moment, contradicting 'had to wait'.
was leaving.misconception: Confuses past continuous (in-progress) with an already-completed prior event.

has left.whyFails: Present perfect cannot combine with a past time frame like 'when I arrived'.
has left.misconception: Uses present perfect, mixing a present-relevance tense into a past narrative.

explain.why: 'Belong' expresses a permanent state of possession. Therefore, the present simple is required, even if the context is the present.
explain.rule: Stative verbs like 'belong', 'own', 'believe', and 'know' usually do not take the -ing form.
explain.memory: States are not continuous: use 'belong', 'own', and 'believe' without -ing.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

is belonging.whyFails: 'Belong' is a stative verb expressing a permanent relationship, not an action in progress, so it cannot take continuous form.
is belonging.misconception: Assumes present time always requires present continuous.

belonging.whyFails: 'This house belonging to my grandparents' has no finite verb, so the sentence is left incomplete.
belonging.misconception: reduces the sentence to a fragment: an -ing form with no finite verb to carry the tense

is being belonged.whyFails: 'Belong' is not used in the passive at all, and stative verbs reject continuous forms.
is being belonged.misconception: Forces a passive continuous structure onto an intransitive stative verb.

explain.why: 'Could have taken' indicates that the job was actually available as an option in the past, but it was not taken.
explain.rule: 'Could have' + 3rd form means a possibility in the past that did not actually happen.
explain.memory: 'Could have' means the door was open, but no one walked through it.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

should have taken.whyFails: The sentence isn't criticizing the choice, only stating that the option existed and was declined: that's 'could have', not 'should have'.
should have taken.misconception: Confuses missed opportunity with retrospective advice/criticism.

were able to take.whyFails: 'Were able to' implies the action was actually carried out, contradicting 'you turned it down'.
were able to take.misconception: Confuses expressing a past possibility with reporting a completed achieved ability.

can take.whyFails: The event is entirely in the past (the offer and refusal already happened), so a present modal is time-inconsistent.
can take.misconception: Uses present modal for a past hypothetical situation.

explain.why: Because it mentions an 'official notice', the most formal register is required. 'May' is the modal for permission commonly used in that register.
explain.rule: Use 'may' for permission in formal registers. 'Can' is usually used for permission in casual conversation. Both are valid, but the registers differ.
explain.memory: Official announcements use formal modals.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

can.whyFails: While grammatically possible in speech, 'can' reads as too informal for an official regulatory notice; 'may' is the conventional formal choice.
can.misconception: Assumes 'can' is equally acceptable in formal written permission notices.

could.whyFails: 'Could' softens into a hypothetical or past sense, which doesn't fit a standing present rule.
could.misconception: Uses the past/tentative form of 'can' for a present-tense rule.

might.whyFails: 'Might' expresses uncertainty about likelihood, not an official grant of permission.
might.misconception: Confuses formal permission with weak possibility.

explain.why: 'Were I to resign' is a formal inverted form of 'If I were to resign', with 'were' moved to the front.
explain.rule: For standard hypothetical situations (Second Conditional): Use 'if' + Verb 2. Example: If I were to win the lottery, I would travel. For formal/literary versions (Inversion without 'if'): The word 'if' is REMOVED, and 'Were' is placed at the very beginning of the sentence! Pattern: 'Were' + Subject + 'to' + base verb. Example: Were I to win the lottery, I would travel (the meaning is exactly the same, just much more formal). 💡 QUICK RULE: With 'if' ➡️ If + Subject + were to + Verb 1. Without 'if' (formal inversion) ➡️ Were + Subject + to + Verb 1 (the word 'if' must be removed!). If there is 'be' without an action verb ➡️ Were + Subject + [adjective/noun] (example: Were I you).
explain.memory: 'Were I to ...' is a formal inverted form of 'If I were to ...'.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

If were I to.whyFails: Inverted conditionals replace 'if' with subject-verb inversion; combining both is redundant and ungrammatical.
If were I to.misconception: Adds 'if' to a structure that already signals conditionality through inversion.

I were to.whyFails: Without either 'if' or inversion (verb-first), the clause is not marked as conditional at all.
I were to.misconception: Drops the inversion, leaving a non-inverted fragment without 'if'.

Was I to.whyFails: Formal inverted second conditionals require 'were', not 'was', regardless of subject.
Was I to.misconception: Uses 'was' instead of the subjunctive 'were' required in formal hypothetical inversion.

explain.why: 'Arrives' is present simple. This form is typically used after 'as soon as' even if the arrival is in the future.
explain.rule: Time conjunctions can be 'when', 'as soon as', 'before', 'after', 'until', or 'once'. In these time clauses, use the present simple. 'Will' is usually placed in the main clause.
explain.memory: After 'as soon as', the present simple still carries a future meaning.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

will arrive.whyFails: After 'as soon as', English normally uses present simple for future reference; 'will' belongs in the main clause.
will arrive.misconception: duplicates future marking inside the time clause

arrived.whyFails: The call and arrival are still future events, so past simple does not fit the timeline.
arrived.misconception: shifts the time clause into a completed past event

would arrive.whyFails: Nothing in the context creates an unreal condition or a past reporting frame requiring 'would'.
would arrive.misconception: treats a real future sequence as hypothetical or future-in-the-past

explain.why: 'Had' matches the past keyword 'last week' and completes the structure required around 'our roof repaired'. Everything is in the past tense.
explain.rule: Difference between Simple Passive vs. Causative: 1. Simple Passive: The subject is the victim or direct recipient of the action. Pattern: 'be + Verb 3'. Example: My phone was stolen or The window was broken. 2. Causative: The subject asks, pays, or tells someone else/an expert to do something for them. Pattern: 'have / get + object + Verb 3'. Example: I had my car repaired (I had my car serviced at a shop—the car didn't service itself, but a mechanic did the work). 💡 QUICK RULE: Passive event regarding the subject ➡️ was/were + Verb 3 (example: My car was damaged). Asking/paying for someone else's service ➡️ have / get + object + Verb 3 (example: I got my car fixed). After the object in causative ➡️ The verb is always Verb 3!
explain.memory: Simple passive uses 'was' or 'were'; asking someone else uses 'had' + the object + past participle.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

were.whyFails: 'Were roof repaired' is not a valid passive construction; the causative pattern needs 'had' + object + past participle to show the subject arranged it.
were.misconception: Treats the sentence as simple passive ('the roof was repaired') rather than causative.

have been.whyFails: 'Have been' doesn't fit the past time marker 'last week' and isn't the causative auxiliary pattern.
have been.misconception: Mixes present perfect passive auxiliary into a past-time causative sentence.

was.whyFails: 'We was' is a subject-verb agreement error, and simple passive still doesn't capture the causative 'arranged for someone' meaning.
was.misconception: Attempts simple past passive but misapplies subject-verb agreement and structure.

explain.why: 'The suspect is believed to have left ...' is a personal passive pattern: the person, then 'is believed', then the 'to' form.
explain.rule: Personal reporting passive: subject + 'is' or 'are' + 'believed', 'thought', or 'said' + 'to' form, not 'that'.
explain.memory: The person + 'is believed' + 'to', not 'that'.
explain.avoid: Write the full form, not just the base word.

is believed that.whyFails: Once the person is the grammatical subject ('The suspect is believed...'), the structure must continue with a to-infinitive, not 'that'.
is believed that.misconception: Blends the personal passive subject pattern with the impersonal 'that'-clause pattern.

it is believed to.whyFails: 'It' would duplicate the subject role already filled by 'the suspect', creating two subjects for one clause.
it is believed to.misconception: Adds a redundant impersonal 'it' when the sentence already has a personal subject.

believed to.whyFails: Without 'is', there's no finite verb to carry the passive structure, leaving the sentence ungrammatical.

explain.why: The reporting verb is 'said', so the form is past. The standard shift from 'can' is 'could'.
explain.rule: If direct speech uses a modal auxiliary verb (can, will, may, must): When reported in the past (Reported Speech with said/told), the modal form MUST shift to the past: - 'can' shifts to could. Example: “I can swim” ➡️ He said he could swim. - 'will' shifts to would. Example: “I will help” ➡️ She said she would help. - 'may' shifts to might. - 'must' / 'have to' shifts to had to. 💡 QUICK RULE: In indirect speech (past) ➡️ Change can ➡️ could, will ➡️ would. Modals that are already past (could, would, should, might) ➡️ Remain the same, do not change again. After a modal (could/would) ➡️ The verb following it remains a plain base verb (Verb 1)!
explain.memory: There is 'said', so the modal is shifted to the past form.
explain.avoid: Check the tense of the reporting verb before shifting the modal.

can.whyFails: With a past reporting verb ('said'), 'can' regularly backshifts to 'could' in standard reported speech.
can.misconception: Assumes modals don't need to shift in reported speech.

cans.whyFails: Modal verbs never take an -s ending; this form doesn't exist in English.
cans.misconception: Treats the modal as a regular verb that takes -s for third person.

will can.whyFails: English does not allow two modal verbs in sequence; 'will' and 'can' cannot combine this way.
