For reported speech with a past reporting verb (said / told): The tense of the utterance must shift one step back into the past (backshift). Verb 1 shifts to Verb 2, “am/is” becomes “was”, “will” becomes “would”, and “can” becomes “could”. Example: He said that he was happy.
Difference between Say and Tell: With “said”, follow directly with the clause (She said that...). With “told”, you MUST mention the listener (She told me that...).

💡 QUICK FORMULA:
Past reporting verb (said/told) ➡️ Tenses inside shift back one step (V1 ➡️ V2, will ➡️ would, can ➡️ could).
With a listener ➡️ Use told + person (example: told me, not said me ❌).
Without mentioning a person ➡️ Use said (that).
explain.memory: Note the backshift: in indirect speech, the verb tense shifts back one step into the past.
explain.avoid: Find the original verb, then shift it exactly one step into the past.

lives.whyFails: 'Said' is past, so 'lives' should move back to 'lived'.

has lived.whyFails: Present simple shifts to past simple, not to the present perfect.
has lived.misconception: backshift target confused with present perfect

would live.whyFails: 'Would' is the backshift of 'will'; the original sentence has no 'will'.
would live.misconception: tense category changed instead of shifted one step back

explain.why: A prohibition becomes “told + person + not to + verb”: told us not to touch.
explain.rule:
For direct commands: Use a command or prohibition verb. Example: “Open the door!” or “Don't touch that!”.
For reported commands: Use “told” or “asked” + the person + “to” (or “not to”).
Positive command: Use “to + base verb”. Example: The teacher told us to open the book.
Negative prohibition: Use “not to + base verb” (the word “not” must come before “to”). Example: Mum told me not to touch the wet paint.

💡 QUICK RULE:
Telling someone to do something ➡️ told / asked + person + to + Verb 1.
Prohibiting / “Don't” ➡️ told / asked + person + not to + Verb 1.
Strictly forbidden ➡️ Do not use don't to or to don't ❌!
explain.memory: Note the command: imperative sentences in indirect speech are connected using the base verb preceded by the marker to.
explain.avoid: Hear a command? Rephrase it as “told someone (not) to do”.

that we don't touch.whyFails: Commands are reported with an infinitive, not a 'that' clause.
that we don't touch.misconception: applies the statement-reporting pattern ('that' clause) to an imperative

didn't touch.whyFails: 'Didn't touch' reports what happened, not what Mum ordered.
didn't touch.misconception: backshifts as if reporting a past statement rather than a command

don't touch.whyFails: The direct imperative cannot be pasted after 'told us'; it needs 'not to'.
don't touch.misconception: leaves the original imperative form unchanged, without integrating it into reported speech

explain.why: The speaker is amazed by the view and expects agreement, so they use a negative question: “Isn't it beautiful?”.
explain.rule: Negative questions (Isn't / Don't / Didn't …?) = the speaker expects a “yes” answer.
explain.memory: Note the purpose of the question: negative questions are used to seek agreement when you are sure the listener shares your opinion.
explain.avoid: Already sure and just want agreement? Start with a negative auxiliary verb.

Is.whyFails: 'Is it beautiful?' is a neutral question; the speaker clearly already thinks so.
Is.misconception: uses a neutral positive question form, missing the speaker's implied surprise/assumption

Doesn't.whyFails: 'Beautiful' is an adjective after 'be', so the auxiliary is 'is', not 'does'.
Doesn't.misconception: uses the 'be' auxiliary instead of the 'do' auxiliary needed for the main verb 'sleep'

Wasn't.whyFails: The view is in front of them now, so the past 'wasn't' does not fit.
Wasn't.misconception: uses present-tense negative auxiliary in a context that requires the past tense to match 'last night'

explain.why: The report was made a week later, so “tomorrow” shifts to “the next day”.
explain.rule: Time shifts in reported speech: today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the day before.
explain.memory: Note the shifts in time and place: in indirect speech, deictic words shift away from the original time of conversation.
explain.avoid: Ask: does “tomorrow” still refer to the same day relative to today? If not, shift it.

tomorrow.whyFails: 'Tomorrow' would mean the day after the report, not the Saturday Dina meant.
tomorrow.misconception: leaving the original deictic time word unchanged despite the shift in reporting time

yesterday.whyFails: 'Yesterday' points backwards from now; Dina was talking about a day after Friday.
yesterday.misconception: misreading the original 'today' as if it referred to the day after speaking

next day.whyFails: The phrase needs 'the': the next day / the following day.
next day.misconception: producing an incomplete deictic shift missing the demonstrative

explain.why: “Every day” and the official time make this a fixed schedule, so use the present simple “opens”.
explain.rule: Present simple for fixed schedules: “the train leaves”, “the museum opens”, “the class starts”.
explain.memory: Schedule → present simple.
explain.avoid: Printed on a schedule or board? Use the present simple.

is opening.whyFails: Present continuous is for personal arrangements, not an official daily time.
is opening.misconception: using present continuous, associated with personal arrangements, for a fixed external timetable

is going to open.whyFails: 'Going to' shows an intention or prediction; a fixed timetable is just stated as a fact.
is going to open.misconception: using 'going to' for intention/prediction rather than an externally fixed schedule

will have opened.whyFails: Future perfect means 'finished before a point'; the sentence gives a regular opening time.
will have opened.misconception: using future perfect, which describes completion before a reference point, not the scheduled departure itself

explain.why: The promise was reported in the past, so “will” becomes “would”: said he would help.
explain.rule: If direct speech uses a modal auxiliary verb (can, will, may, must): When reported in the past (Reported Speech with said/told), the modal form MUST shift to the past: - 'can' shifts to could. Example: “I can swim” ➡️ He said he could swim. - 'will' shifts to would. Example: “I will help” ➡️ She said she would help. - 'may' shifts to might. - 'must' / 'have to' shifts to had to. 💡 QUICK RULE: In indirect speech (past) ➡️ Change can ➡️ could, will ➡️ would. Modals that are already past (could, would, should, might) ➡️ Remain the same, do not change again. After a modal (could/would) ➡️ The verb following it remains a plain base verb (Verb 1)!
explain.memory: Note the modal shift: modal auxiliaries shift to their corresponding past forms in indirect speech.
explain.avoid: Is there a modal in the direct speech? Swap it for its past counterpart and keep the verb in its base form.

will.whyFails: After past 'said', 'will' normally shifts back to 'would'.
will.misconception: Assumes modals don't need to shift in reported speech.

wills.whyFails: Modals never take -s; 'wills' treats 'will' like an ordinary verb.
wills.misconception: Treats the modal as a regular verb that takes -s for third person.

would to.whyFails: A modal is followed directly by the base verb; there is no 'to' after 'would'.
would to.misconception: Attempts to stack two modals together.

explain.why: Yes/no questions are reported using “if” plus statement word order, and “are” shifts back to “was”.
explain.rule: If a direct question: Use question structure with an auxiliary verb at the front. Example: “Do you like milk?” or “Where do you live?”. If reported (Reported Question): The sentence structure CHANGES to a normal statement (Subject + Verb) without auxiliary verbs like 'do/does/did' and without a question mark. Yes/No questions: Connect with 'if' or 'whether' (meaning 'whether or not'). Example: He asked me if I liked milk (Not if did I like ❌). 💡 QUICK RULE: Yes/No questions ➡️ Use asked + if / whether + Subject + Verb. Word order ➡️ Must be normal sentence structure: Subject first, then verb (do not use do/does/did!). Tenses ➡️ Must shift to the past (example: is becomes was, like becomes liked).
explain.memory: Note the question type: yes/no questions in indirect speech are connected using the conjunction whether/if.
explain.avoid: Can the direct question be answered with yes or no? Start the report with “if”.

was I.whyFails: It keeps the question inversion and has no 'if' to introduce the reported question.
was I.misconception: keeps direct-question inversion and omits if/whether

that I was.whyFails: 'That' reports statements; a yes/no question needs 'if' or 'whether'.
that I was.misconception: uses 'that' for a yes/no reported question

if was I.whyFails: 'If' is right, but the subject must come before the verb: if I was.
if was I.misconception: adds whether but retains auxiliary-subject inversion

explain.why: Grandfather is there as a patient, so use “in hospital” without an article.
explain.rule: No article is used if the institution is used for its primary purpose: in hospital, at school, in prison. Use “the” for the physical building.
explain.memory: Note the status of the visit: distinguish between receiving treatment as a patient and simply visiting the location.
explain.avoid: Ask: patient, student, or prisoner? If yes, omit the article.

the hospital.whyFails: 'The hospital' points to a building; being a patient there uses no article.
the hospital.misconception: focuses on a particular building instead of institutional attendance

a hospital.whyFails: 'A hospital' introduces one random building, not Grandpa's stay as a patient.
a hospital.misconception: introduces one unspecified building rather than the attendance idiom

hospitals.whyFails: Plural 'hospitals' turns one stay into a general destination.
hospitals.misconception: turns one routine of attendance into a generic plural destination

explain.why: “The film” is a thing and the object of “watched”, so “that” is appropriate, and it can even be omitted.
explain.rule:
In relative clause connectors (who, which, that):
1. If the connector functions as the SUBJECT (followed immediately by a verb): The connector MUST BE WRITTEN; it cannot be omitted! Example: The man who called you is here (Incorrect: The man called you is here ❌).
2. If the connector functions as the OBJECT (followed by a new subject + verb): The connector CAN BE DELETED entirely without changing the meaning! Example: The book (that) I read yesterday was great ➡️ simply write The book I read yesterday was great.

💡 QUICK FORMULA:
Connector followed immediately by a VERB ➡️ who / which / that is mandatory (cannot be deleted!).
Connector followed by a NEW SUBJECT (I, you, we, she...) ➡️ The connector CAN BE DELETED (e.g., the movie we watched).
explain.memory: Note the role: if the relative pronoun acts as the object of the action, it can naturally be omitted.
explain.avoid: Try deleting the pronoun. If the sentence still works, then “that” or leaving it blank is correct.

who.whyFails: 'Who' is for people; a film needs 'that' or 'which'.
who.misconception: Uses a personal relative pronoun for a non-human antecedent.

whose.whyFails: 'Whose' shows possession; nothing belongs to anyone here.
whose.misconception: uses possessive 'whose' where the clause needs an object relative pronoun or nothing at all

what.whyFails: 'What' is never a relative pronoun after a noun in English.
what.misconception: Uses 'what' as a relative pronoun, a common cross-linguistic transfer error.

explain.why: “Easier” is a comparative form, so the intensifier must be a comparative intensifier: a lot easier.
explain.rule: Use much, far, a lot, or a bit before comparative forms; do not use very.
explain.memory: Note the degree intensifier: place an intensifier before the comparative form to emphasize a large difference.
explain.avoid: See -er or “more”? Choose much / far / a lot.

very.whyFails: 'Very' goes before a plain adjective (very easy), not before 'easier'.
very.misconception: Transfers the common absolute-adjective intensifier 'very' onto a comparative form.

so.whyFails: 'So' needs a 'that' clause or an exclamation and does not modify 'easier'.
so.misconception: Uses 'so', which needs a following 'that'-clause or exclamatory context, as a plain intensifier before a comparative.

too.whyFails: 'Too' means 'more than is good' and cannot strengthen a comparative.
too.misconception: Uses 'too' (meaning excessive) as if it were a neutral intensifier.

explain.why: Echo questions follow statement word order and replace the surprising part with “where”: He's moving where?
explain.rule: Echo questions: repeat the statement, place the question word at the position of the surprising information, and use a rising intonation.
explain.memory: Note the purpose: echo questions are used to ask for confirmation or to express surprise at news just heard.
explain.avoid: Copy the sentence, then place the question word exactly where the surprising word was.

where is he.whyFails: It turns the echo into a standard inverted question and repeats the subject.
where is he.misconception: Forms a standard inverted question instead of echoing the statement's structure.

to where is he moving.whyFails: It rebuilds the whole question instead of echoing the surprising part.
to where is he moving.misconception: Fully reformulates the question with standard word order rather than echoing.

moving where.whyFails: It repeats the verb fragment; the echo already has 'He's moving' before the gap.
moving where.misconception: Uses a gerund fragment instead of the statement's original verb form.

explain.why: “This month” has not ended yet, so a completed action within it uses the present perfect: have read.
explain.rule: Present perfect with unfinished time periods: today, this week, this month, this year.
explain.memory: Note the time period: if the current timeframe has not ended and the results can still increase, use the perfect aspect.
explain.avoid: Ask: is the time period still open? If yes, use have/has + past participle (Verb 3).

read.whyFails: Past simple closes the period, but 'this month' is still going on.
read.misconception: Uses past simple because a specific number of emails is mentioned.

was reading.whyFails: Past continuous shows an action in progress, not two completed books.
was reading.misconception: Uses past continuous to describe a series of completed actions.

am reading.whyFails: Present continuous means right now; 'already' shows the books are finished.
am reading.misconception: Uses present simple, ignoring that the sentence reports completed past actions within the current period.

explain.why: “Will” already occupies the modal slot, so ability is expressed using “be able to”: will be able to speak.
explain.rule: Ability after another modal or “to”: use be able to (will be able to, hope to be able to).
explain.memory: Expressing future ability: after "will", you must use "be able to" (never "will can")!
explain.avoid: Need “can” after will, must, or to? Swap it for “be able to”.

will can.whyFails: 'Can' is a finite modal and cannot follow 'will'.
will can.misconception: places the finite modal 'can' after infinitive 'to'

will could.whyFails: 'Could' is also a finite modal; two modals never stack.
will could.misconception: uses a finite past/conditional modal in a non-finite slot

will being able to.whyFails: After 'will' the verb is the bare form 'be', not 'being'.
will being able to.misconception: uses a gerund-participle where a bare infinitive is required

explain.why: No one answered, and “them” is a pronoun, so the form is “none of them”.
explain.rule:
If a quantifier (like both, all, none, some, neither) meets an object pronoun (them, us, you) directly: You MUST insert the word “of” in between! Example: both of them, all of us (it is a major error to write both them ❌ or all them ❌).
Difference: Use “both of” (the two) or “neither of” (neither of the two) specifically for a group of EXACTLY TWO PEOPLE/THINGS. Use “all of” or “none of” if the number is THREE OR MORE.

💡 QUICK RULE:
Quantifier + object pronoun (them, us, you) ➡️ MUST have of in the middle (e.g., both of them, all of us).
Specifically for a group of 2 people / things ➡️ Use both of (positive) or neither of (negative).
Group of 3 people or more ➡️ Use all of or none of.
explain.memory: Note the pronoun: quantifiers preceding an object pronoun require a connecting preposition.
explain.avoid: Is there them / us / you / it after the quantifier? Insert “of”.

no.whyFails: 'No' goes directly before a noun (no friends), never before 'them'.
no.misconception: drops 'of' and ignores the explicitly two-person set

any of.whyFails: 'Any of them answered' is not negative; the sentence needs 'none of'.
any of.misconception: drops 'of' and reverses the affirmative meaning

explain.why: “Ones” replaces the plural noun “shoes” after the adjective “bigger”: any bigger ones.
explain.rule: Adjective + one (singular) / ones (plural) replaces a noun that has already been mentioned.
explain.memory: Avoid noun repetition: place a plural pronoun substitute after the adjective to make the sentence more concise.
explain.avoid: Count the replaced noun: singular → one, plural → ones.

one.whyFails: 'Shoes' is plural, so the substitute must be plural 'ones'.
one.misconception: picks plural 'ones' to replace a single noun

them.whyFails: 'Them' cannot follow an adjective like 'bigger'; it stands alone.
them.misconception: uses definite 'it' after 'a new' where the indefinite substitute 'one' is needed

shoes ones.whyFails: It repeats the noun and adds the substitute on top of it.
shoes ones.misconception: repeats the replaced noun and stacks the substitute 'one' after it

explain.why: The door is never locked, so the meaning of “forget to lock” (an unperformed task) is needed.
explain.rule: Forget/remember + to-infinitive = obligation/task. Forget/remember + -ing = memory of something that already happened.
explain.memory: Pay attention to execution: forgetting to do something results in the action never being performed at all.
explain.avoid: Ask: did the action happen? If not, use “forget to”.

locking.whyFails: 'Forget locking' would mean I have no memory of locking it; here the locking never happened.
locking.misconception: applies the 'future duty' pattern ('remember to do') to a sentence that is actually recalling a completed past action

lock.misconception: uses the bare infinitive, which isn't a valid pattern after 'remember' in either meaning

to have locked.whyFails: The perfect infinitive is not used after 'forget' for a simple undone task.
to have locked.misconception: applies a perfect to-infinitive after 'remember', which English does not use for recalling a past action

explain.why: “Every year” shows continuous increase, so the double comparative form “more and more expensive” is appropriate.
explain.rule: Gradual change: -er and -er (bigger and bigger) or more and more + long adjective.
explain.memory: Pay attention to the relationship of change: arrange balanced comparisons to show that the change in one thing is directly proportional to another.
explain.avoid: Still changing? Double the comparative form.

more expensive than.whyFails: 'Than' needs a second item to compare with; nothing follows it here.
more expensive than.misconception: treats a continuous, ongoing change as a single fixed-point comparison

the most expensive.whyFails: A superlative names the top item; it cannot show a change 'every year'.
the most expensive.misconception: confuses a progressive change over time with a superlative ranking among multiple items

expensiver and expensiver.whyFails: 'Expensive' is a long adjective, so it takes 'more', not -er.
expensiver and expensiver.misconception: uses a single comparative with 'more' for a short adjective, and frames it as a comparison to a norm rather than ongoing change

explain.why: There is no specific source, so the impersonal passive “It is said that…” is used.
explain.rule: Impersonal reporting structure: “It” + “is/was” + “said/believed/thought” + “that” + clause.
explain.memory: Pay attention to the source of the news: if the statement is general and the original speaker is not mentioned, prioritize the passive report pattern with an introductory subject.
explain.avoid: Reporting a rumor or general belief? Start with “It is said / believed that”.

They are saying.whyFails: A vague 'they' in the continuous does not report a general belief.
They are saying.misconception: using active voice with a vague 'they' plus an incorrect continuous form for a general belief

It says.whyFails: 'It says' makes 'it' the speaker; the house does not say anything.
It says.misconception: treating 'it' as an active subject capable of believing

Is said.whyFails: The impersonal passive needs the dummy subject 'it' in front.
Is said.misconception: dropping the required dummy subject 'it' from the impersonal passive pattern

explain.why: The result receives the action, so use the passive infinitive “to be published” after “expected”.
explain.rule:
When following verbs that require an infinitive (such as expect to, hope to, need to, deserve to) in the passive voice:
After the word “to”, you MUST pair it with a plain “be” + past participle (Verb 3).
Compare:
- Active: I expect to meet them.
- Passive: Everyone expects to be treated fairly (not to treat and not to being treated).

💡 QUICK FORMULA:
Passive meaning (being acted upon) after “to” ➡️ Must use to be + Verb 3.
Active form (performing the action) ➡️ Use to + Verb 1.
The form of 'be' ➡️ Must be a plain be (forbidden to use to been or to being!).
explain.memory: Pay attention to the subject receiving the action: after a modal or expectation verb, apply the correct basic passive form.
explain.avoid: Ask: does the subject perform the action or receive the action? Receives → to be + participle.

to publish.whyFails: The results cannot publish anything; they are published, so the passive is needed.
to publish.misconception: using active infinitive when the subject (the policy) cannot perform the announcing itself

publishing.whyFails: 'Expected' takes a to-infinitive, not a gerund.
publishing.misconception: using a gerund where an infinitive pattern after 'expected' is required

to be publishing.whyFails: The continuous form adds an ongoing meaning that does not fit a single release.
to be publishing.misconception: adding continuous aspect to the passive infinitive unnecessarily

explain.why: Lifting the box was a failed effort, so the meaning of “tried to lift” is needed.
explain.rule: Try + to-infinitive = make an effort (difficult). Try + -ing = test a method to see the result.
explain.memory: Observe the effort: distinguish between trying hard to overcome a difficulty and simply testing a new method.
explain.avoid: Difficult and perhaps impossible? Use “try to”.

lifting.whyFails: 'Try lifting' means testing lifting as one method; here the speaker struggled and failed at the effort.
lifting.misconception: using 'try to' (make a difficult effort) where 'try -ing' (experiment with a solution) is meant

lift.misconception: using the bare infinitive after 'try', which isn't a valid pattern

having lifted.whyFails: A perfect gerund says the lifting is already done, which contradicts 'I couldn't'.
having lifted.misconception: using a perfect gerund, implying the action is already completed

explain.why: Catching the train was possible but didn't happen, and there is no criticism, so “could have caught” is appropriate.
explain.rule: Could have + past participle (Verb 3) expresses a past opportunity that was not taken. Should have + Verb 3 expresses criticism or regret about a past action.
explain.memory: Could have, but didn't.
explain.avoid: Ask: possible but not done, and no one is to blame? Use “could have”.

should have caught.whyFails: 'Should have' criticises a mistake, but the speaker says 'no regrets'.
should have caught.misconception: Confuses missed opportunity with retrospective advice/criticism.

were able to catch.whyFails: 'Were able to' reports that we actually caught it, but we did not.
were able to catch.misconception: Confuses expressing a past possibility with reporting a completed achieved ability.

can catch.whyFails: 'Can' is present; the missed train is in the past.
can catch.misconception: Uses present modal for a past hypothetical situation.

explain.why: “Philippines” is a plural country name, so use “the”: the Philippines.
explain.rule: No article for most countries (Japan, Indonesia). “The” is used for plural or descriptive names (the Philippines, the United States, the UK).
explain.memory: Pay attention to geographical names: country names generally do not take an article except for plural or union country names.
explain.avoid: Does the country name end in -s or contain words like States/Kingdom/Republic? Use “the”.

a.whyFails: A country name is not a countable noun that takes 'a'.
a.misconception: Treats the country name as an ordinary countable noun needing an indefinite article.

an.whyFails: 'An' is chosen by the following vowel sound, but no indefinite article fits a country name.
an.misconception: Applies the indefinite article rule based on the following vowel sound, ignoring that country names don't take indefinite articles at all.

[no article].whyFails: Most countries take no article, but plural names like the Philippines and the Netherlands need 'the'.
[no article].misconception: Overgeneralizes the common 'no article before country names' rule to every country name.

explain.why: The noun “reason” is always followed by “for”: the reason for his decision.
explain.rule:
Some abstract nouns in English have FIXED preposition pairs that cannot be interchanged:
1. “reason for”: Example: What is the reason for your delay? (Not reason to ❌ or reason of ❌).
2. “solution to” / “answer to”: Example: We need a solution to this problem (Not solution for ❌).
3. “effect on”: Example: The effect on our health.

💡 QUICK FORMULA:
The word “reason” ➡️ Must be paired with reason for.
The word “solution / answer” ➡️ Must be paired with solution to / answer to.
The word “effect / impact” ➡️ Must be paired with effect on.
explain.memory: Pay attention to the noun: pair the noun with its standard fixed preposition.
explain.avoid: Keep the noun and its preposition as a single package: reason for.

of.whyFails: 'Of' feels natural because it links many nouns, but 'reason' takes 'for'.
of.misconception: Assumes 'of' universally links a noun to what it relates to.

to.whyFails: 'To' belongs to 'solution to' or 'answer to', not to 'reason'.
to.misconception: Transfers the preposition pattern from a related phrase like 'search for' onto 'solution'.

about.whyFails: 'About' introduces a topic; 'reason' needs the cause marker 'for'.
about.misconception: Borrows a preposition associated with 'deal with' or 'cope with' a problem.

explain.why: The exam was last week, so the regret uses the past perfect: If only I had studied harder.
explain.rule:
If imagining a current condition: Use “If only” + Verb 2. Example: If only I had more time today.
If regretting a past event that has already passed: Use “If only” + had + Verb 3. Example: If only I had studied harder last week (I wish I had studied harder last week, but my grades are already out).

💡 QUICK RULE:
Regret past event (with: yesterday, last week, last year) ➡️ If only + had + Verb 3.
Regret doing something ➡️ If only + hadn't + Verb 3.
explain.memory: It is too late to regret: “If only I had…”.
explain.avoid: Is there a past time word along with “if only”? Step back one more tense: had + participle.

studied.whyFails: Past simple after 'if only' is for a present wish; 'last week' makes this a past regret.
studied.misconception: staying with the past simple, which cannot mark the unreal past that regret needs

would have studied.whyFails: 'Would have' is the result-clause shape; it does not follow 'if only'.
would have studied.misconception: moving the 'would have' shape of the result clause into the wish clause itself

have studied.whyFails: Present perfect ties the studying to now, but 'last week' is finished.
have studied.misconception: choosing the present perfect, which ties the missed reading to the present moment

explain.why: The speaker is annoyed by their neighbor's habit and wants it to change, so use “wish he would turn”.
explain.rule:
When wishing about a situation or one's own desire: Use “wish + Verb 2”. Example: I wish I had a car.
When annoyed / irritated by SOMEONE ELSE'S BEHAVIOR and wanting them to stop: Use “wish + someone else + would” + base verb. Example: I wish he would turn down the music.

💡 QUICK RULE:
Annoyed by someone else's behavior ➡️ wish + [that person] + would + base verb.
Not for oneself ➡️ Do not use I wish I would (because one's own behavior can be controlled directly).
explain.memory: Annoyed by someone else's behavior: “I wish he would stop!”.
explain.avoid: Complaining about something others keep doing? “I wish they would…”

turned.whyFails: 'Wish + past simple' describes a state; a complaint about repeated behaviour uses 'would'.
turned.misconception: treats a complaint about repeated behaviour as a wished-for state with wish + past simple

turns.misconception: keeping the present tense after 'wish', reading the situation as a real current fact

will turn.misconception: puts future 'will' after 'wish' instead of using the past tense or 'would' form required in wish clauses

explain.why: “Get used to” is followed by -ing: get used to getting up at five.
explain.rule:
For a past habit that HAS STOPPED NOW: Use “used to” + base verb (Verb 1). Example: I used to play marbles (I played often in the past, but I never do now).
If you ARE ACCUSTOMED TO IT NOW (it feels normal and familiar): Use “be” (am/is/are) before it and it must be followed by an -ing verb. Example: I am used to living in Jakarta.
For the PROCESS of becoming accustomed: Use “get used to” + -ing verb. Example: He is getting used to waking up early.

💡 QUICK RULE:
Used to do something but not anymore (no be) ➡️ used to + Verb 1.
Accustomed to it now (with am/is/are) ➡️ be used to + Verb-ing.
The process of adapting ➡️ get used to + Verb-ing.
explain.memory: Pay attention to the habit: distinguish past habits that have stopped from current adaptation processes or feelings of familiarity.
explain.avoid: Is there “be” or “get” before “used to”? The next verb ends in -ing.

get.whyFails: The 'to' in 'get used to' is a preposition, so the verb after it takes -ing.
get.misconception: reads the 'to' in 'be used to' as an infinitive marker, copying the past-habit pattern

got.whyFails: A past form cannot follow the preposition 'to'.
got.misconception: slots a finite past form after the preposition 'to' in 'be used to'

be getting.whyFails: 'Be' treats the 'to' as an infinitive marker; the pattern needs -ing directly.
be getting.misconception: inserts infinitive 'be' after 'used to' although this 'to' is a preposition needing -ing

explain.why: “Would rather” is directly followed by the base verb: I'd rather drink tea.
explain.rule: Would rather + base verb (+ than + base verb). Prefer + to-infinitive or -ing.
explain.memory: Pay attention to the choice: after an expression of preference using a modal, place the base verb directly without 'to'.
explain.avoid: After “rather”, write the verb without anything in front of it.

to drink.whyFails: 'Prefer to drink' takes 'to', but 'would rather' takes the bare verb.
to drink.misconception: generalizes the to-infinitive to 'would rather' on the model of 'prefer to'

drinking.whyFails: -ing belongs to 'prefer drinking', not to 'would rather'.
drinking.misconception: imports the gerund complement of 'prefer' into the 'would rather' pattern

drank.whyFails: A past form is not used after 'would rather' when the speaker talks about their own preference now.
drank.misconception: backshifts to a past form after 'would rather' although no second subject intervenes

explain.why: Meeting at six was the promise, and it failed, so “was supposed to meet” expresses an unfulfilled expectation.
explain.rule: Be supposed to + verb = expected or promised. The “be” changes according to tense (is/was).
explain.memory: Pay attention to the initial plan: express a past plan or promise that should have been carried out but in reality fell short.
explain.avoid: Always say be + supposed to as a single package: is supposed to, was supposed to.

supposed to.whyFails: 'Supposed to' always needs a form of 'be' in front: was supposed to.

supposes to.whyFails: 'Suppose' as an ordinary verb means 'think'; the expectation pattern needs 'be supposed to'.
supposes to.misconception: treats 'suppose' as an ordinary present-tense verb instead of the passive pattern 'be supposed to'

was supposing to.whyFails: 'Supposed' here is a fixed participle and never takes -ing.
was supposing to.misconception: forces a progressive onto the fixed passive participle 'supposed'

explain.why: “It's time we” is followed by the unreal past even though the meaning is present: it's time we went home.
explain.rule: It's (high) time + subject + past tense (Verb 2) = something should happen now or is already overdue.
explain.memory: Pay attention to the urgency: expressions of urgent time are always followed by a sentence with a past meaning to show lateness.
explain.avoid: See “it's time” with a subject following it? Put the verb in the past tense (Verb 2).

go.whyFails: After 'it's time + subject', the verb takes the unreal past, not the present.
go.misconception: keeps a present-tense verb after 'it's high time', calquing 'it's already time' plus a present verb

will go.whyFails: 'Will' does not follow 'it's time we'; the fixed form is past simple.
will go.misconception: marks the clause after 'it's high time' with future 'will' because the action is still to come

are going.whyFails: The continuous describes what is happening; 'it's time' says what should happen.
are going.misconception: uses the present progressive after 'it's high time' as if the action were already under way

explain.why: He has never lived there, so the unreal comparison uses the past tense (Verb 2): as if he lived there.
explain.rule: As if / as though + past tense (Verb 2) = unreal now. + present tense = possibly true.
explain.memory: Pay attention to reality: assumptions that contradict reality apply the past tense in the explanatory part.
explain.avoid: Is the comparison clearly false? Shift the verb one step back into the past.

lives.whyFails: The present suggests it might be true, but 'he has never left our village' shows it is not.
lives.misconception: keeps the real-possibility present after 'as if' although the sentence denies the comparison

has lived.whyFails: Present perfect reports real experience; he has no such experience.
has lived.misconception: reads 'as if' as reporting genuine experience with the present perfect

would live.whyFails: 'Would' belongs in a result clause, not inside an 'as if' clause.
would live.misconception: puts conditional 'would' inside the 'as if' clause as if it were a result clause

explain.why: Missing the bus was in the past, but “now” makes the result present, so use “would be”.
explain.rule: Mixed conditional: If + past perfect (past cause), would + base verb (present effect).
explain.memory: Pay attention to the tense combination: connect a past action whose effect still influences the current situation.
explain.avoid: Look for “now” or “today” in the result clause: this indicates would + base verb, not would have.

would have been.whyFails: 'Would have been' describes a past result, but 'now' places the result in the present.
would have been.misconception: places the result in the unreal past instead of the present

was.whyFails: Plain past 'was' states a real fact; the situation is imaginary.
was.misconception: uses a past form without the modal required in the result clause

had been.whyFails: 'Had been' is the if-clause form; the result clause needs 'would'.
had been.misconception: repeats past perfect in the main clause

explain.why: In formal style, “if” is omitted and “had” moves before the subject: Had we received the warning.
explain.rule:
For standard past hypothetical (Third Conditional): Use “If” + had + Verb 3. Example: If I had known about the test, I would have studied. For the formal/literary version (inversion without “if”): The word “if” is REMOVED, and the auxiliary “Had” is moved to the very front before the subject! Pattern: “Had” + Subject + Verb 3. Example: Had I known about the test, I would have studied (the meaning is identical, but the tone is more elegant and formal).

💡 QUICK RULE:
With “if” ➡️ If + Subject + had + Verb 3.
Without “if” (inversion) ➡️ Had + Subject + Verb 3 ('if' is forbidden!).
The result clause remains the same ➡️ Always use would have + Verb 3.
explain.memory: Type 3 conditional inversion: remove "If", invert the subject to "Had we known"!
explain.avoid: Delete “if”, then swap the positions of the subject and “had”; nothing else changes.

If we had received.whyFails: This is correct in neutral style, but the target form drops 'if' and inverts 'had'.
If we had received.misconception: mixing formal inversion with the conjunction 'if' at the same time

We had received.whyFails: Without 'if' or inversion, this is just a statement, not a condition.
We had received.misconception: using normal subject-verb order, missing the inversion signal

Had received we.whyFails: Only 'had' moves to the front; the subject stays before the participle.
Had received we.misconception: using the result-clause auxiliary structure at the start of the if-clause

explain.why: “Rarely” at the beginning causes the auxiliary verb to move before the subject: the auxiliary “have” moves before “I”.
explain.rule:
Normal word order: Emphatic adverbs are placed in the middle of the sentence. Example: I have never seen such a view. Inverted word order (auxiliary before subject for emphasis): When negative adverbs (Never, Rarely, Seldom, Hardly, Not only) are placed at the START of a sentence, the auxiliary and subject MUST BE INVERTED exactly like a question! Example: Never have I seen such a view or Rarely did she speak.

💡 QUICK RULE:
Negative adverb at the start (Never, Rarely, Seldom, Not only) ➡️ Must invert: Adverb + Auxiliary + Subject + Verb.
Past tense without an auxiliary ➡️ Insert did + Subject + Verb 1 (e.g., Rarely did he come).
Do not use normal order if the adverb is at the front ➡️ It is a major error: Never I have seen ❌!
explain.memory: Inversion of negative words at the start of a sentence (Rarely): invert the auxiliary before the subject: "Rarely have I seen"!
explain.avoid: Rarely/never at the front? Structure it like a question: have I seen.

I have seen.whyFails: After fronted 'Rarely', the auxiliary must come before the subject.
I have seen.misconception: Fronts the negative adverbial without applying the required subject-auxiliary inversion.

I saw.whyFails: No inversion and no auxiliary: the fronted adverb demands both.
I saw.misconception: Fronts 'Never' with no auxiliary at all, ignoring both the inversion rule and the need for 'have' with 'before'.

saw I.whyFails: Inversion uses an auxiliary (have/do/did), not the main verb alone.
saw I.misconception: Places 'never' after the auxiliary instead of at the very front of the sentence.

explain.why: “Only when…” at the front causes the auxiliary verb to move before the subject: did the boats leave.
explain.rule:
Normal sentence structure: The limiting phrase “only” is in its usual position. Example: We realized the truth only after reading the letter. If the limiting phrase “Only” (Only after, Only when, Only then, Only by) is placed at the START of a sentence: The main clause following it MUST BE INVERTED exactly like a question (Auxiliary + Subject + Verb)! Example: Only after reading the letter did we realize the truth (Not we realized ❌).

💡 QUICK RULE:
Start with Only after / Only when / Only then ➡️ The following main clause must be inverted (auxiliary precedes subject).
Past tense ➡️ Use did + Subject + Verb 1 (e.g., Only then did I know).

explain.why: “It was raining” is the reason we stayed inside, so use “because”.
explain.rule:
Distinguishing REASON (cause) vs. RESULT (effect):
1. Reason / Cause: Use “Because” before the cause. Example: We stayed home because it rained.
2. Result / Effect: Use “so” before the resulting event (placed in the middle of the sentence, preceded by a comma). Example: It rained, so we stayed home.

💡 QUICK RULE:
Before the cause of an event ➡️ Use because.
Before the impact / result of an event ➡️ Use , so.
Prohibition ➡️ Do not combine both in one sentence (incorrect: Because it rained so we stayed home ❌).

explain.avoid: Ask yourself: is the part after it a reason or a result? Is it a full sentence or just a noun phrase?

explain.why: I feel very unwell, so the cold today is worse than before, and the special form of “bad” is “worse”.
explain.rule: “good” → “better” → “the best”; “bad” → “worse” → “the worst”. No -er, no “more”.
explain.memory: Pay attention to irregular adjectives: these have unique comparative forms where the entire word changes.
explain.avoid: Before adding -er or “more”, check: is the adjective “good” or “bad”?

badder.whyFails: It is not an English word; bad has its own special form.
badder.misconception: regular -er ending forced onto an irregular adjective

more bad.whyFails: It uses more, but bad has its own special form.
more bad.misconception: regular 'more + adjective' pattern applied to an irregular adjective

more worse.whyFails: It marks the comparison twice; the special form alone is enough.
more worse.misconception: doubles the comparative marking by putting 'more' before an adjective already ending in '-er'

explain.why: Two things are compared with “than”, and the “more” form of “good” is “better”.
explain.rule: “good” → “better” → “the best”; “bad” → “worse” → “the worst”. No -er, no “more”.
explain.memory: Pay attention to irregular adjectives: these have unique comparative forms where the entire word changes.
explain.avoid: Before adding -er or “more”, check: is the adjective “good” or “bad”?

more good.whyFails: It uses more, but good has its own special comparative.
more good.misconception: regular 'more + adjective' pattern applied to an irregular adjective

best.whyFails: It is for the top of a group, but than compares only two ways to travel.
best.misconception: superlative 'best' used where 'than' demands a comparative

good.whyFails: It does not compare, but than needs a comparative.
good.misconception: base adjective used without comparative marking
